headline: Shah Rukh Khan turns 61 as Bollywood stars celebrate the 'King' ahead of new film
description: Suhana Khan, Kajol, Kareena Kapoor, Anil Kapoor among others lead tributes as SRK unveils 'King' song 'Tu Mil Jaaye'
author: Life And Style Desk
article_text:
Bollywood superstar Shah Rukh Khan marked his 61st birthday with a special treat for fans, unveiling Tu Mil Jaaye, the first song from his much-awaited film King, as birthday wishes poured in from family, friends and colleagues across the film industry.

From his daughter Suhana Khan sharing a heartfelt tribute to Kajol, Kareena Kapoor Khan, Shilpa Shetty and Anil Kapoor celebrating the actor, the occasion highlighted the affection he continues to command across Bollywood.

The celebrations also extended to Mumbai, where fans gathered outside his residence, Mannat, to mark the birthday of the man fondly known as Bollywood's King Khan.

Screengrab: suhanakhan2, theshilpashetty/Instagram

Shah Rukh's daughter Suhana Khan took to Instagram to celebrate her father, sharing a picture of the poster of his upcoming film King. Keeping her message short and sweet, she wrote, "Happy birthday king."

Shilpa Shetty also shared a loving birthday tribute on her Instagram Story, calling Shah Rukh her forever Baazigar. Sharing a picture with the superstar, she wrote, "To the one and only King Khan. My forever Baazigar, who wins in every heartbeat. Happy birthday, wishing you endless love, laughter, great health and happiness always."

Screengrab: sonamkapoor, kajol/Instagram

Sonam Kapoor also wished the superstar with a warm message on her Instagram Story. "Happy happy birthday Shah Rukh Khan. Lots and lots of love to you, always! Can't wait to see you in King," she wrote.

Kajol, who shares a much-loved on-screen history with Shah Rukh, also sent him birthday wishes. Sharing a message on her Instagram Story, she wrote, "Happy Birthday SRK! Stay the absolute rockstar that you are. Sending you the biggest hug today!"

View this post on Instagram

Kareena Kapoor Khan also joined the celebrations with a special Instagram post, sharing a glimpse connected to King. Her caption read, "Happy Birthday King. The forever Ruler of the kingdom. Let's dance together... Can't wait. 24-12-26."

Her message also sparked excitement about what appears to be a special dance collaboration in the upcoming film.

Anil Kapoor, meanwhile, shared a nostalgic birthday message on X, reflecting on the years of friendship and memories he shares with Shah Rukh.

He wrote, "Happy Birthday, Shah Rukh! ❤️ Years of laughter, countless memories and you haven't lost an ounce of that charm or madness and clearly neither of us is counting the years. Here's to many more. Jaldi milte hai, Lots of love always!"

Filmmaker Karan Johar also joined the celebrations, sharing a picture of Shah Rukh looking dapper and noticeably fit for his upcoming film. Praising the actor's appearance, Karan wrote, "61? Never looked this fine."

Screengrab: karanjohar/Instagram

Shah Rukh also shared a moment of his own with fans.

Taking to X, the actor posted a photograph of the Bandra-Worli Sea Link illuminated with his pictures and birthday wishes.

He thanked Google Gemini for the special tribute, writing, "Dost ho toh Google Gemini jaisa.. Thank you for the KING-sized love always.... had to sneak out for a drive to get this photo ha ha.."

View this post on Instagram

The birthday celebrations also drew crowds to Mannat, where fans gathered to celebrate their favourite superstar. The residence was adorned with visuals from King, alongside a special message from Shah Rukh thanking his admirers.

The actor also marked the occasion by unveiling Tu Mil Jaaye, the first song from King, giving fans an early glimpse of the film's music.

Featuring Shah Rukh Khan and Deepika Padukone, the romantic track is composed by Sachin-Jigar, with vocals by Arijit Singh and Madhubanti Bagchi. British singer Ed Sheeran has also contributed an English rap to the song.

The release offers fans their first musical glimpse into the much-awaited film, which promises a blend of romance and action.

View this post on Instagram

Directed by Siddharth Anand, King also stars Suhana Khan, Abhishek Bachchan, Rani Mukerji, Anil Kapoor and others. The film is scheduled to arrive in cinemas worldwide on December 24, 2026, making it one of the most anticipated releases of the Christmas season.

With tributes from Bollywood colleagues, celebrations outside Mannat and a musical surprise from King, Shah Rukh's 61st birthday proved to be a celebration befitting the superstar.

headline: Sadiq pinpoints flaws in Babar's batting
description: Former opener suggests technical adjustments to help Pakistan’s star regain form
author: Alam Zeb Safi
article_text:
KARACHI: Former Pakistan Test opener Sadiq Mohammad has identified several technical flaws in Babar Azam's batting, pointing to his early shot selection, footwork, batting stance and failure to judge deliveries outside off stump as areas requiring attention.

In an interview with The Express Tribune Sadiq, who also played county cricket for Gloucestershire, drew on his own experience of overcoming similar batting difficulties to offer Babar a series of technical suggestions. He believes adjustments to Test captain's stance, footwork and timing could help him rediscover his scoring touch.

Recalling how he overcame his own problems, Sadiq said he had struggled with dismissals in the third-slip, gully and backward-point areas during his county career. He discussed the issue with his elder brother Wazir Mohammad, who watched him bat in the nets at Birmingham and suggested technical adjustments.

Sadiq said the advice worked, as he went on to score a century in his very next innings against Warwickshire.

Identifying Babar's first problem, Sadiq believes the right-hander plays his shots too early, with the bat away from his body and his front left toe.

He also highlighted Babar's batting stance, which he believes makes it difficult for the batsman to judge the width of deliveries outside off stump.

According to Sadiq, Babar's back foot touches the off-stump line when he makes contact with the ball. This, he believes, allows bowlers to exploit the sixth-stump line with away-swinging deliveries, tempting Babar into chasing balls outside off stump.

Sadiq suggested that Babar change his guard from leg stump to fourth-leg stump and move his right back foot towards a position between leg and middle stump as the bowler approaches the umpire. He believes this adjustment would encourage bowlers to target the stumps rather than exploit the space outside off stump.

Another concern, according to Sadiq, is Babar's tendency to play the ball too early instead of allowing it to come closer to his body.

He believes this causes Babar's off-side shots to travel towards gully, third slip and backward point. Making contact around six inches away from his left-foot toe, Sadiq said, changes the bat's position from a closed face to an open face, resulting in sliced shots that travel behind square in the air rather than along the ground.

He also pointed out that Babar does not transfer enough body weight onto his front foot while driving, preventing him from directing the ball towards the front of square.

Sadiq further stressed the importance of watching the ball make contact with the bat, saying Babar's failure to do so is another reason his cover drives travel behind square.

article_html:
KARACHI: Former Pakistan Test opener Sadiq Mohammad has identified several technical flaws in Babar Azam's batting, pointing to his early shot selection, footwork, batting stance and failure to judge deliveries outside off stump as areas requiring attention.

In an interview with The Express Tribune Sadiq, who also played county cricket for Gloucestershire, drew on his own experience of overcoming similar batting difficulties to offer Babar a series of technical suggestions. He believes adjustments to Test captain's stance, footwork and timing could help him rediscover his scoring touch.

Recalling how he overcame his own problems, Sadiq said he had struggled with dismissals in the third-slip, gully and backward-point areas during his county career. He discussed the issue with his elder brother Wazir Mohammad, who watched him bat in the nets at Birmingham and suggested technical adjustments.

Sadiq said the advice worked, as he went on to score a century in his very next innings against Warwickshire.

Identifying Babar's first problem, Sadiq believes the right-hander plays his shots too early, with the bat away from his body and his front left toe.

He also highlighted Babar's batting stance, which he believes makes it difficult for the batsman to judge the width of deliveries outside off stump.

According to Sadiq, Babar's back foot touches the off-stump line when he makes contact with the ball. This, he believes, allows bowlers to exploit the sixth-stump line with away-swinging deliveries, tempting Babar into chasing balls outside off stump.

Sadiq suggested that Babar change his guard from leg stump to fourth-leg stump and move his right back foot towards a position between leg and middle stump as the bowler approaches the umpire. He believes this adjustment would encourage bowlers to target the stumps rather than exploit the space outside off stump.

Another concern, according to Sadiq, is Babar's tendency to play the ball too early instead of allowing it to come closer to his body.

He believes this causes Babar's off-side shots to travel towards gully, third slip and backward point. Making contact around six inches away from his left-foot toe, Sadiq said, changes the bat's position from a closed face to an open face, resulting in sliced shots that travel behind square in the air rather than along the ground.

He also pointed out that Babar does not transfer enough body weight onto his front foot while driving, preventing him from directing the ball towards the front of square.

Sadiq further stressed the importance of watching the ball make contact with the bat, saying Babar's failure to do so is another reason his cover drives travel behind square.

On timing and contact, he advised Babar to make contact with the ball in front of his left front toe while playing on the front foot, keeping his back bent to ensure the ball travels along the ground. He said the same principle should apply when playing off the back foot, with contact aligned with the front-foot toe.

Sadiq believes regular practice in the nets, particularly with the suggested change in stance and foot positioning, could help Babar direct most of his attacking and defensive shots towards the front of square.

Despite identifying these shortcomings, Sadiq expressed confidence in Babar's ability to return to his previous form.

"Babar, in my view, you are still a very good batsman. I suggest you work on my tips, and you will be the same Babar again. For a world-class batsman like you, it should not be difficult to apply these changes in your next outing. Go out and get it right," Sadiq signed off.

Former Pakistan captain Mohammad Yousuf also wrote on X the other day that Babar should be sent to England and Australia to work on his batting flaws.

Sadiq also appreciated Yousuf saying former batsman’s suggestion is almost right, but he as an opening batsman has different suggestion.

headline: New cyberattack on supermarket fridges sweeps across Europe
description: Attack raises temperatures in refrigerator, freezer units at dozens of stores, forcing supermarkets to discard food
author: Reuters
article_text:
A hacking attack on European supermarkets spread across the continent on Monday, hitting fridges and ​freezers from Sweden to Belgium and forcing stores to throw away food in an incident that echoed a similar attack in France last month.

The attack, which raised temperatures in refrigerator and ‌freezer units at dozens of stores, hit supermarket groups Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt in Belgium and Luxembourg, as well as Swedish grocers ICA and Coop. Furniture-to-meatballs retailer IKEA also saw at least one store affected.

"Everything is destroyed," Engla Ingwall, sales manager at an ICA franchise store in Stockholm, told Reuters during a visit to the store on Monday, adding the attack occurred at 2 am (0100 GMT) but was only noticed hours later.

"There has been a cyberattack and all our freezers reached 50 degrees (Celsius)."

A spokesperson for privately held ICA said the company ​was aware that a "limited number of stores were affected by an incident overnight, which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems".

The latest incidents follow an attack in France last month when police said hackers seized control of ​cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, causing fires and food losses. Ahold also reported a cybersecurity incident to police last month.

While no one has claimed responsibility for either attack, ⁠the incidents have heightened concerns among European authorities about hybrid threats to infrastructure amid growing security tensions since Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Moscow has repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage or hybrid warfare operations. Reuters could not establish who was ​behind Monday's attacks or whether they were linked to the incidents in France.

"It is not known who is behind this attack, and it may never be determined," said Katrien Eggers, spokesperson for Belgium's Centre for Cybersecurity, adding she was concerned ​about the growing number of incidents, in part due to AI.

"All IT systems are potentially vulnerable, and AI can now be used to successfully exploit these weaknesses — especially by sophisticated actors," she said.

'Retail is an easy target'

From refrigerators and heating systems to security cameras and alarms, an expanding range of devices once largely mechanical can now be monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals.

At least some of the refrigerator units affected on Monday used temperature control technology from Danish firm Danfoss that was also targeted in the French ​attack. The firm said it had been working with customers to implement fixes.

The European Commission said the latest incidents highlighted how digital threats are becoming increasingly disruptive.

"They are a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine ​consumers' confidence in it – a warning that we must take seriously," said EU commissioner for agriculture Christophe Hansen. "The repeated occurrence of these cyberattacks is deeply concerning."

A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, said five shops ‌had their ⁠fridge systems attacked.

In Ireland, wholesaler Musgrave said the incident affected systems in 13 of its SuperValu stores, forcing it to remove some chilled and frozen products from sale.

"Our monitoring systems alerted us to the issue, and we took immediate action," it said in a statement. "Our investigation is ongoing."

Tom Hegel, a researcher at cybersecurity firm SentinelOne, said such attacks were typically linked to extortion, political motives or nation-state operations, with the absence of financial demands in recent cases pointing instead to sabotage.

"Retail is an easy target because retail chains run enormous estates of refrigeration controllers, building management systems, door access panels and point-of-sale gear," he said, adding it was hard to trace hackers targeting such systems.

"An attacker who logs into ​an exposed control panel leaves almost nothing behind ... A teenager ​and an intelligence service would look much the ⁠same from the defender's side."

'It's very scary'

Carrefour, which was badly hit in last month's French attack, said 15 of its 700 stores in Belgium were affected. IKEA said one store in Belgium had been impacted and that it could not rule out disruptions at other locations.

Privately held Swedish grocery chain Coop said that 7 of its 800 stores were ​affected by a cyber incident involving unauthorised tampering with its refrigeration systems. It said Danfoss was among its suppliers.

Luc De Laet, founder and owner of Belgian butchery ​chain De Laet & Van Haver, said ⁠he was woken at 3:30 am by an employee telling him there was a problem. He rushed to his store south of Antwerp and found the fridges turned up as high as 18 C.

He estimated the incident ruined about €15,000 ($16,800) worth of meat.

"It's very scary. They are hacking the system that is doing the registration of the temperature, and they can program it at a distance," he told Reuters, adding that it was infuriating to throw away so much food.

De Laet said he believed ⁠the hackers were ​trying to destabilise European economies. He had contacted police but did not know whether an investigation had been launched.

"I only have two words ​for them: wake up, please, because there's something going on," he said.

A hacking attack on European supermarkets spread across the continent on Monday, hitting fridges and ​freezers from Sweden to Belgium and forcing stores to throw away food in an incident that echoed a similar attack in France last month.

The attack, which raised temperatures in refrigerator and ‌freezer units at dozens of stores, hit supermarket groups Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt in Belgium and Luxembourg, as well as Swedish grocers ICA and Coop. Furniture-to-meatballs retailer IKEA also saw at least one store affected.

"Everything is destroyed," Engla Ingwall, sales manager at an ICA franchise store in Stockholm, told Reuters during a visit to the store on Monday, adding the attack occurred at 2 am (0100 GMT) but was only noticed hours later.

Fridges and freezers at supermarkets in Belgium, Sweden, Luxembourg and Ireland warmed overnight, about three weeks after France.

"There has been a cyberattack and all our freezers reached 50 degrees (Celsius)."

A spokesperson for privately held ICA said the company ​was aware that a "limited number of stores were affected by an incident overnight, which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems".

The latest incidents follow an attack in France last month when police said hackers seized control of ​cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, causing fires and food losses. Ahold also reported a cybersecurity incident to police last month.

Read: Investigators hunt French supermarket fridge hackers, no claim of responsibility

While no one has claimed responsibility for either attack, ⁠the incidents have heightened concerns among European authorities about hybrid threats to infrastructure amid growing security tensions since Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Moscow has repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage or hybrid warfare operations. Reuters could not establish who was ​behind Monday's attacks or whether they were linked to the incidents in France.

"It is not known who is behind this attack, and it may never be determined," said Katrien Eggers, spokesperson for Belgium's Centre for Cybersecurity, adding she was concerned ​about the growing number of incidents, in part due to AI.

"All IT systems are potentially vulnerable, and AI can now be used to successfully exploit these weaknesses — especially by sophisticated actors," she said.

'Retail is an easy target'

From refrigerators and heating systems to security cameras and alarms, an expanding range of devices once largely mechanical can now be monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals.

At least some of the refrigerator units affected on Monday used temperature control technology from Danish firm Danfoss that was also targeted in the French ​attack. The firm said it had been working with customers to implement fixes.

The European Commission said the latest incidents highlighted how digital threats are becoming increasingly disruptive.

Read More: French supermarket fridges hacked

"They are a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine ​consumers' confidence in it – a warning that we must take seriously," said EU commissioner for agriculture Christophe Hansen. "The repeated occurrence of these cyberattacks is deeply concerning."

A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, said five shops ‌had their ⁠fridge systems attacked.

In Ireland, wholesaler Musgrave said the incident affected systems in 13 of its SuperValu stores, forcing it to remove some chilled and frozen products from sale.

"Our monitoring systems alerted us to the issue, and we took immediate action," it said in a statement. "Our investigation is ongoing."

Tom Hegel, a researcher at cybersecurity firm SentinelOne, said such attacks were typically linked to extortion, political motives or nation-state operations, with the absence of financial demands in recent cases pointing instead to sabotage.

"Retail is an easy target because retail chains run enormous estates of refrigeration controllers, building management systems, door access panels and point-of-sale gear," he said, adding it was hard to trace hackers targeting such systems.

— Politics UK (@PolitlcsUK) November 2, 2026

"An attacker who logs into ​an exposed control panel leaves almost nothing behind ... A teenager ​and an intelligence service would look much the ⁠same from the defender's side."

'It's very scary'

Carrefour, which was badly hit in last month's French attack, said 15 of its 700 stores in Belgium were affected. IKEA said one store in Belgium had been impacted and that it could not rule out disruptions at other locations.

Privately held Swedish grocery chain Coop said that 7 of its 800 stores were ​affected by a cyber incident involving unauthorised tampering with its refrigeration systems. It said Danfoss was among its suppliers.

Luc De Laet, founder and owner of Belgian butchery ​chain De Laet & Van Haver, said ⁠he was woken at 3:30 am by an employee telling him there was a problem. He rushed to his store south of Antwerp and found the fridges turned up as high as 18 C.

He estimated the incident ruined about €15,000 ($16,800) worth of meat.

"It's very scary. They are hacking the system that is doing the registration of the temperature, and they can program it at a distance," he told Reuters, adding that it was infuriating to throw away so much food.

De Laet said he believed ⁠the hackers were ​trying to destabilise European economies. He had contacted police but did not know whether an investigation had been launched.

"I only have two words ​for them: wake up, please, because there's something going on," he said.

headline: 4 polio immunisation workers abducted in K-P’s Tank
description: TTP abducts two others from Azam Warsak, but subsequently lets them go
author: Ramzan Seemab
article_text:
Four polio immunisation workers were abducted by unidentified armed men after being fired upon in Khyber-Paktunkhwa’s Tank district, while two other members of a polio vaccination team, who had been kidnapped in Azam Warsak, were subsequently released.

According to details, the abduction incident in Tank occurred in a village located in the Sheikh Attar union council, where unidentified armed men abducted the four polio vaccination workers.

Police said the gunmen took all the workers to an undisclosed location.

Police have launched an investigation into the incident.

Further details about the identity of the perpetrators and the whereabouts of the kidnapped workers were not immediately available.

In a separate incident, two members of a polio vaccination team were abducted by armed men in the Azam Warsak area of Lower South Waziristan. However, both vaccinators were later released.

Sources said the suspects were affiliated with the proscribed Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan.

The incidents have raised concerns over the security of polio vaccination teams working in the remote region, where they continue to face threats while carrying out the immunisation campaigns.

A day earlier, the National Emergency Operations Centre (NEOC) for Polio Eradication confirmed Pakistan's seventh polio case of the year, reported from K-P. The infected child was a 13-month-old girl belonging to Jan Baz Union Council in Bara tehsil, the NEOC said.

It was the second polio case reported from Khyber district this year.

Of the seven cases reported across the country so far this year, six have emerged from K-P and one from Sindh, according to the NEOC.

headline: PTI's Barrister Salman Safdar meets Imran, Bushra Bibi in Adiala jail
description: The meeting took place for 40 minutes
author: Imran Asghar
article_text:
Barrister Salman Safdar on Monday met Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) founder Imran Khan and his wife Bushra Bibi at Adiala jail.

Imran has been in custody since August 2023, serving a sentence in a £190 million corruption case. He also faces pending trials under the Anti-Terrorism Act in connection with protests on May 9, 2023. He and Bushra Bibi remain incarcerated in Rawalpindi's Adiala jail. They were sentenced on December 20, 2025, to 17 years in prison in the Toshakhana-II case, which pertains to allegations that the couple unlawfully retained a Bulgari jewellery set gifted by the Saudi crown prince during an official visit to Saudi Arabia.

The PTI has been consistently protesting and demanding that the authorities allow Imran's weekly meetings with his friends, relatives and legal team.

In a post on X today, Barrister Safdar said he met the PTI founder and Bushra Bibi for about 40 minutes for a meeting arranged by the jail authorities at 4:30pm.

According to Barrister Safdar, the meeting took place after multiple requests and marked his first meeting with Imran in seven months and with Bushra in 11 months.

“The session was insufficient to cover all cases/legal matters,” the legal counsel lamented in the social media post, adding that the two him of their health and the conditions in which they were being kept in prison.

Safdar added that both had also conveyed fresh instructions regarding certain legal matters and ongoing cases.

The lawyer did not provide further details about the specific legal instructions discussed during the meeting.

The Islamabad High Court (IHC) on September 2 directed the jail authorities to ensure meaningful human interaction, family access, exercise, reading material and other facilities for Imran and his wife, Bushra.

The court held that lawful incarceration did not authorise the avoidable deprivation of human dignity.

In August, the Supreme Court ordered that Imran be shifted to Shifa International Hospital for treatment and directed the government to arrange weekly meetings between him and his family.

On June 18, the IHC had directed Islamabad's advocate general to ensure that a meeting was arranged within seven days between Imran, Bushra and their legal counsel to facilitate the completion of legal formalities and the prosecution of appeals against their conviction in the £190 million reference case.

Barrister Safdar last held a meeting on April 9 with Imran for legal consultation regarding the £190m case.

He stated that Adiala jail authorities had facilitated his meeting in compliance with IHC orders, adding that the meeting lasted 60 minutes.

The SC had previously ordered the formation of a medical team to examine Imran's eye after Barrister Safdar's report quoted the PTI founder as stating that "only 15%" vision remained in his right eye. The court also directed that both the medical examination and telephonic contact with his children be completed before February 16.

Barrister Salman Safdar on Monday met Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) founder Imran Khan and his wife Bushra Bibi at Adiala jail.

Imran has been in custody since August 2023, serving a sentence in a £190 million corruption case. He also faces pending trials under the Anti-Terrorism Act in connection with protests on May 9, 2023. He and Bushra Bibi remain incarcerated in Rawalpindi's Adiala jail. They were sentenced on December 20, 2025, to 17 years in prison in the Toshakhana-II case, which pertains to allegations that the couple unlawfully retained a Bulgari jewellery set gifted by the Saudi crown prince during an official visit to Saudi Arabia.

The PTI has been consistently protesting and demanding that the authorities allow Imran's weekly meetings with his friends, relatives and legal team.

In a post on X today, Barrister Safdar said he met the PTI founder and Bushra Bibi for about 40 minutes for a meeting arranged by the jail authorities at 4:30pm.

Imran Khan’s lawyer, Barrister Salman Safdar, was finally allowed to meet with him in Adiala Jail for 40 minutes after 7 months.

“Today at 4:30 PM, Adiala Jail authorities facilitated a 40-minute meeting with Mr. Imran Khan and his wife, Bushra Imran. After repeated… pic.twitter.com/a2vgIk6fjo

— PTI (@PTIofficial) November 2, 2026

According to Barrister Safdar, the meeting took place after multiple requests and marked his first meeting with Imran in seven months and with Bushra in 11 months.

“The session was insufficient to cover all cases/legal matters,” the legal counsel lamented in the social media post, adding that the two him of their health and the conditions in which they were being kept in prison.

Safdar added that both had also conveyed fresh instructions regarding certain legal matters and ongoing cases.

The lawyer did not provide further details about the specific legal instructions discussed during the meeting.

https://t.co/jAjfJULunS

— PTI (@PTIofficial) November 2, 2026

The Islamabad High Court (IHC) on September 2 directed the jail authorities to ensure meaningful human interaction, family access, exercise, reading material and other facilities for Imran and his wife, Bushra.

The court held that lawful incarceration did not authorise the avoidable deprivation of human dignity.

In August, the Supreme Court ordered that Imran be shifted to Shifa International Hospital for treatment and directed the government to arrange weekly meetings between him and his family.

On June 18, the IHC had directed Islamabad's advocate general to ensure that a meeting was arranged within seven days between Imran, Bushra and their legal counsel to facilitate the completion of legal formalities and the prosecution of appeals against their conviction in the £190 million reference case.

Barrister Safdar last held a meeting on April 9 with Imran for legal consultation regarding the £190m case.

Read: Imran in good health, high spirits: lawyer

He stated that Adiala jail authorities had facilitated his meeting in compliance with IHC orders, adding that the meeting lasted 60 minutes.

The SC had previously ordered the formation of a medical team to examine Imran's eye after Barrister Safdar's report quoted the PTI founder as stating that "only 15%" vision remained in his right eye. The court also directed that both the medical examination and telephonic contact with his children be completed before February 16.

headline: Govt slashes petrol by Rs3.4, high-speed diesel by Rs7.76
description: New petrol price is Rs374.51 while HSD is Rs395.2
author: Zaigham Naqvi
article_text:
The federal government on Monday slashed the price of petrol by Rs3.4 per litre and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs7.76 for November 3.

A press release from the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority said the new petrol price was Rs374.51 while HSD was Rs395.2.

Earlier today, the government announced that oil refineries would bear a burden of Rs15 billion per month, which would allow petrol to be sold Rs15 cheaper than it was in the global market amid the US-Israeli war on Iran.

On July 17, the government announced a new pricing mechanism under which petroleum product prices would be reviewed and notified daily, replacing the weekly pricing mechanism, as renewed tensions between the United States and Iran continued to drive volatility in global oil markets and raise concerns over fuel supplies.

On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif announced a special relief scheme offering Rs100 per litre off petrol for motorcycles, three-wheeler rickshaws and cars with engines up to 800cc, in an attempt to shield lower-income consumers from the impact of rising petroleum prices.

Under the proposal, an estimated 11.8 million beneficiaries would be covered. Around 10 million two-wheeler users and 800,000 three-wheeler users would be entitled to relief on 20 litres of fuel per month, translating into a maximum monthly benefit of Rs2,000 per beneficiary.

Another one million users of cars up to 800cc would receive relief on 30 litres per month, providing them with a maximum benefit of Rs3,000 each.

On Sept 17, the government reintroduced austerity and fuel conservation measures amid rising fuel prices, tightening business operating hours and restricting public events.

Under the measures, notified with immediate effect, shops, markets, shopping malls, bazaars, departmental stores, grocery stores, general stores and kiryana shops would close by 9pm throughout the week, according to a notification issued by the Cabinet Division.

Marriage halls, marquees and other commercial venues hosting festive events would close by 10pm, while restaurants, cafes, eateries, food outlets and standalone fruit and vegetable shops would be allowed to operate until 11pm. Takeaway and home delivery services would remain exempt from the timing restrictions.

headline: Trump could launch nuclear strike on Iran within days, claims Tucker Carlson
description: Warns a nuclear explosion at Pickaxe Mountain can contaminate the Gulf, threaten water supply of 100 million people
author: Anadolu Agency
article_text:
US commentator Tucker Carlson claimed on Sunday that the Trump administration could be days away from launching a nuclear strike on Iran, alleging that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was pressuring President Donald Trump to authorise an attack on a suspected nuclear site in central Iran.

In a lengthy post on X, Carlson identified the potential target as Pickaxe Mountain, where Israeli intelligence allegedly believed Iran had resumed its nuclear enrichment program.

Carlson is a conservative political commentator and former Fox News host whose program, Tucker Carlson Tonight, aired from 2016 to 2023.

He now hosts an independent political show on X, where he regularly comments on US foreign policy and international affairs.

Carlson claimed conventional US weapons could not penetrate the estimated 300 feet of solid granite protecting underground tunnels at the site, leaving a nuclear strike as the only military option.

"Bibi (Netanyahu) calls Trump about it every day," Carlson quoted an unnamed informed observer as saying.

Carlson argued that Netanyahu's political survival was driving his push for further military action. He claimed Netanyahu needs Trump's intervention to secure a 61-seat majority in the Knesset following the latest election results, warning that otherwise he could lose power and face investigations and possible imprisonment.

He also alleged that Netanyahu has been pressing senior US officials, including Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and US Central Command chief Adm Brad Cooper, to resume major combat operations.

Carlson also claimed that Secretary of State Marco Rubio and CIA Director John Ratcliffe were following Netanyahu's lead.

He further said former president Barack Obama had also opposed the Iran peace agreement being drafted in Doha.

Fears of regional escalation

Carlson said US allies in the Middle East were increasingly concerned about renewed fighting. He claimed Netanyahu secretly travelled to Abu Dhabi on September 27 to persuade the UAE to support a final attack on Iran, but Emirati officials refused.

Warning of the economic consequences, Carlson said eight months of conflict had severely affected Gulf economies, as well as global energy and fertiliser markets. He claimed 11 of the world's approximately 850 oil supertankers were badly damaged in the Strait of Hormuz in October alone.

He also warned that a nuclear explosion at Pickaxe Mountain could contaminate the Gulf and threaten the water supply of around 100 million people.

Carlson argued that a US nuclear strike could establish a dangerous precedent, potentially encouraging Russia to use nuclear weapons against Ukraine, triggering renewed nuclear tensions between India and Pakistan, and prompting North Korea to attack Seoul.

"After the first nuclear strike, World War Three is inevitable. That war would be short and final," he wrote.

He further alleged that the Trump administration had quietly revised US nuclear doctrine since February to make the first use of so-called "battlefield nukes" easier and more likely.

Vance, Witkoff urge Trump to pursue diplomacy

Carlson said Trump could decide by November 7 whether to authorise the use of nuclear weapons, adding that Vice President JD Vance and special envoy Steve Witkoff were urging him to pursue a diplomatic agreement with Tehran.

Although acknowledging that negotiations would be difficult, Carlson said people who had spoken with Iranian decision-makers believed there was a consensus that further conflict would benefit no one and that an agreement was worth pursuing.

He concluded by warning that the consequences of a nuclear strike would extend far beyond Iran, arguing that the international public had been excluded from decisions that could threaten millions of lives.

"Now would be the time for them to speak up," Carlson wrote.

US could strike remaining Iranian nuclear sites 'within 10 minutes'

Carlson's claims follow Trump's remarks to reporters at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida on Saturday that one or two Iranian nuclear facilities remained potential targets and that the US could strike them within 10 minutes.

Trump specifically mentioned Pickaxe Mountain, saying he had military plans for the area, but did not indicate that a nuclear strike had been authorised.

"You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly," he added.

In an October 16 interview with Newsmax, he explicitly ruled out using nuclear weapons against Iran.

Separately, Axios reported that Trump and Netanyahu held a tense phone call on Saturday, citing Israeli and US sources. According to the report, Netanyahu is pushing for renewed military action immediately after Tuesday's US midterm elections, while Trump prefers to allow diplomatic negotiations to continue.

A White House official said the administration does not comment on sensitive military plans, adding that Trump is keeping all options open to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

Secretary of State Rubio has also said no final decision has been made on resuming strikes.

Iran, meanwhile, denies any nuclear activity at the Pickaxe Mountain complex. Its supreme leader has warned Washington and Tel Aviv against launching further attacks.

article_html:
US commentator Tucker Carlson claimed on Sunday that the Trump administration could be days away from launching a nuclear strike on Iran, alleging that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was pressuring President Donald Trump to authorise an attack on a suspected nuclear site in central Iran.

In a lengthy post on X, Carlson identified the potential target as Pickaxe Mountain, where Israeli intelligence allegedly believed Iran had resumed its nuclear enrichment program.

Carlson is a conservative political commentator and former Fox News host whose program, Tucker Carlson Tonight, aired from 2016 to 2023.

Under pressure from Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the Trump administration may be within days of launching a nuclear strike on Iran. The target would be Pickax Mountain in central Iran, where Israeli intelligence claims the Iranian government has restarted its…

— Tucker Carlson (@TuckerCarlson) November 2, 2026

He now hosts an independent political show on X, where he regularly comments on US foreign policy and international affairs.

Carlson claimed conventional US weapons could not penetrate the estimated 300 feet of solid granite protecting underground tunnels at the site, leaving a nuclear strike as the only military option.

Read: Trump says US will strike reported Iranian nuclear site at Pickaxe Mountain 'very heavily'

"Bibi (Netanyahu) calls Trump about it every day," Carlson quoted an unnamed informed observer as saying.

Carlson argued that Netanyahu's political survival was driving his push for further military action. He claimed Netanyahu needs Trump's intervention to secure a 61-seat majority in the Knesset following the latest election results, warning that otherwise he could lose power and face investigations and possible imprisonment.

He also alleged that Netanyahu has been pressing senior US officials, including Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and US Central Command chief Adm Brad Cooper, to resume major combat operations.

Carlson also claimed that Secretary of State Marco Rubio and CIA Director John Ratcliffe were following Netanyahu's lead.

He further said former president Barack Obama had also opposed the Iran peace agreement being drafted in Doha.

Fears of regional escalation

Carlson said US allies in the Middle East were increasingly concerned about renewed fighting. He claimed Netanyahu secretly travelled to Abu Dhabi on September 27 to persuade the UAE to support a final attack on Iran, but Emirati officials refused.

Warning of the economic consequences, Carlson said eight months of conflict had severely affected Gulf economies, as well as global energy and fertiliser markets. He claimed 11 of the world's approximately 850 oil supertankers were badly damaged in the Strait of Hormuz in October alone.

He also warned that a nuclear explosion at Pickaxe Mountain could contaminate the Gulf and threaten the water supply of around 100 million people.

Carlson argued that a US nuclear strike could establish a dangerous precedent, potentially encouraging Russia to use nuclear weapons against Ukraine, triggering renewed nuclear tensions between India and Pakistan, and prompting North Korea to attack Seoul.

"After the first nuclear strike, World War Three is inevitable. That war would be short and final," he wrote.

BIG: Tucker Carlson says Trump may decide by Nov. 7 on a nuclear strike on Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain under Netanyahu’s pressure.

“After the first nuclear strike, World War Three is inevitable,” Carlson wrote.https://t.co/h0UMiAa1YH

— Clash Report (@clashreport) November 2, 2026

He further alleged that the Trump administration had quietly revised US nuclear doctrine since February to make the first use of so-called "battlefield nukes" easier and more likely.

Vance, Witkoff urge Trump to pursue diplomacy

Carlson said Trump could decide by November 7 whether to authorise the use of nuclear weapons, adding that Vice President JD Vance and special envoy Steve Witkoff were urging him to pursue a diplomatic agreement with Tehran.

Although acknowledging that negotiations would be difficult, Carlson said people who had spoken with Iranian decision-makers believed there was a consensus that further conflict would benefit no one and that an agreement was worth pursuing.

He concluded by warning that the consequences of a nuclear strike would extend far beyond Iran, arguing that the international public had been excluded from decisions that could threaten millions of lives.

"Now would be the time for them to speak up," Carlson wrote.

US could strike remaining Iranian nuclear sites 'within 10 minutes'

Carlson's claims follow Trump's remarks to reporters at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida on Saturday that one or two Iranian nuclear facilities remained potential targets and that the US could strike them within 10 minutes.

US President Donald Trump says American forces have destroyed much of Iran's naval, air defense and military capabilities, along with its nuclear infrastructure. He says one or two sites remain, including Pickaxe Mountain, and asserts that the US could destroy them in just 10… pic.twitter.com/RNI2WP5xcM

— Al Arabiya English (@AlArabiya_Eng) November 1, 2026

Trump specifically mentioned Pickaxe Mountain, saying he had military plans for the area, but did not indicate that a nuclear strike had been authorised.

Read More: What is Pickaxe Mountain, the Iranian nuclear-linked site threatened by Trump?

"You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly," he added.

In an October 16 interview with Newsmax, he explicitly ruled out using nuclear weapons against Iran.

Separately, Axios reported that Trump and Netanyahu held a tense phone call on Saturday, citing Israeli and US sources. According to the report, Netanyahu is pushing for renewed military action immediately after Tuesday's US midterm elections, while Trump prefers to allow diplomatic negotiations to continue.

Netanyahu is pressing Trump to resume strikes on Iran immediately after Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections, but Trump wants to give diplomacy more time.

The two held a tense phone call Saturday, described as “tough” by an Israeli source and “direct” by a U.S. source.

Source:… pic.twitter.com/Ux1PREksnD

— Clash Report (@clashreport) November 1, 2026

A White House official said the administration does not comment on sensitive military plans, adding that Trump is keeping all options open to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

Secretary of State Rubio has also said no final decision has been made on resuming strikes.

Iran, meanwhile, denies any nuclear activity at the Pickaxe Mountain complex. Its supreme leader has warned Washington and Tel Aviv against launching further attacks.

"After the first nuclear strike, World War Three is inevitable. That war would be short and final," he wrote.

Carlson's claims follow Trump's remarks to reporters at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida on Saturday that one or two Iranian nuclear facilities remained potential targets and that the US could strike them within 10 minutes.

Trump specifically mentioned Pickaxe Mountain, saying he had military plans for the area, but did not indicate that a nuclear strike had been authorised.

"You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly," he added.

In an October 16 interview with Newsmax, he explicitly ruled out using nuclear weapons against Iran.

Separately, Axios reported that Trump and Netanyahu held a tense phone call on Saturday, citing Israeli and US sources. According to the report, Netanyahu is pushing for renewed military action immediately after Tuesday's US midterm elections, while Trump prefers to allow diplomatic negotiations to continue.

A White House official said the administration does not comment on sensitive military plans, adding that Trump is keeping all options open to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

Secretary of State Rubio has also said no final decision has been made on resuming strikes.

Iran, meanwhile, denies any nuclear activity at the Pickaxe Mountain complex. Its supreme leader has warned Washington and Tel Aviv against launching further attacks.

headline: The ownership disclosure
description: Committee report came in the last week of October and it was damning
author: Muhammad Hamid Zaman
article_text:
Last week, the most prominent news in the higher education sector in the US was that the provost (and the chief academic officer) at Dartmouth College resigned. Dartmouth College is a premier institution of higher learning in the United States and while many readers of this newspaper may not really care about a higher education official of a US institution leaving his post, I believe that the reasons for his departure are relevant beyond the US and worthy of our reflection.

Dr Santiago Schnell, who served as the provost at Dartmouth for just over a year, was a well-regarded scholar in the field of mathematical biology. He had trained at Oxford and prior to his position at Dartmouth, he had worked at Indiana University, University of Michigan and University of Notre Dame. In August and September of this year, two news outlets – Semafor in August and The Dartmouth, the university student newspaper, in September – revealed that Dr Schnell had widely used generative AI in his writing without disclosing its use, including in journals and newspapers where there are clearly laid-out requirements for disclosure, or any use of generative AI is prohibited. When confronted, Dr Schnell acknowledged using AI for 'language refinement' or 'copyediting' but did not elaborate any further. As a result of the detailed story published in The Dartmouth student newspaper, many students and faculty at Dartmouth College were upset at what they saw was the blatant disregard for the university policies. They argued that if the student did such a thing (i.e. use AI and not disclose the use), they would get into serious trouble – so why is it that the chief academic officer can get away with it? There were others who found the entire episode distasteful – and antithetical to creativity, originality and transparency. The movement picked up steam and the university president tasked a faculty-led committee – comprising computer science faculty and humanities faculty – to further look into the matter.

The committee report came in the last week of October and it was damning. Dr Schnell had used generative AI in many of his recent publications, had violated policies of journals and was not forthcoming about those, and did not cooperate with the committee. Soon after the report was sent to the university president, Dr Schnell resigned and left the university.

There are many things to unpack here. First, the remarkable role of student journalists who are determined to hold university leadership to account. They deserve a lot of credit for their work and their commitment. Second, what incensed many people was that there should be same set of rules for everyone, and the faculty should be held to the same standards as they expect the students to abide by. But there is a bigger and perhaps nagging question about the pull of AI. Dr Schnell has had a distinguished career spanning well over two decades when he wrote outstanding papers and made important discoveries. His papers shaped ideas and created new knowledge. Why does someone like that choose to rely on something that takes away creativity and originality? Why does he need to rely on AI for language refinement when he did not need it for twenty something years? What pull does it have? And if someone does believe there is nothing wrong in using AI for 'language refinement' (or more) then why not declare it? Why not be open about it, or perhaps even be proud of it?

These are complex questions and perhaps we will never know the answers. But it is worth reflecting on how the notions of efficiency can force us to compromise the very foundations research, scholarship and inquiry. We should ask on our campuses and beyond: when we choose efficiency, are we OK with giving up creativity, originality and transparency? And should we be comfortable in doing so? Is that a good thing for the enterprise of learning, and society at large? And if not, then what guardrails should we create immediately?

headline: War madness
description: encouraging sign, nonetheless, is that Qatari and Pakistani interlocutors are being heard in Tehran and Washington
author: editorial
article_text:
There is widespread war hysteria despite credible diplomatic maneuvering in the Middle East. The fear of the unknown stems from an impulsive American President, whose Republican party is performing poorly in midterm exit polls. Consequently, it is widely forecast that a new attack on Iran is being planned to distract from domestic political struggles. There are also reports that the Israeli Prime Minister is persuading the White House incumbent to launch "tactical nuclear strikes" against Iran, which remains unrelenting in its refusal to compromise over its enriched uranium. The war criminal has been pushing hard for this barbaric option for quite some time.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei, however, categorically stated yesterday that his country "will not transfer its enriched uranium to a third country", just as Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi once again laid down his preconditions for a thaw. These conditions included lifting the new sanctions imposed after the Islamabad MoU, scaling back the US military presence in the region, and ending the blockade at the mouth of the Arabian Sea.

The encouraging sign, nonetheless, is that Qatari and Pakistani interlocutors are being heard in Tehran and Washington. Araghchi has confirmed that a proposal is currently under discussion through Qatari and Pakistani mediators. This proposal is primarily based on Iran's original seven-day plan, which promises the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz "on the sixth day" if Iran's conditions are met. This is a welcome development that coincides with Vice President Vance's eagerness to open new vistas of dialogue with the Islamic Republic.

With a follow-up meeting expected between the warring sides and the mediators, the rising volatility could certainly be tamed. Saudi Arabia, having put three of its cities on high alert, is keeping its fingers crossed as the Houthis continue to push things over the brink. Likewise, the UAE foresees wider destruction if the region returns to war. This uncertainty can only be addressed if dialogue is recognised as the sole option. Let serenity triumph over insanity.

headline: Police brutality
description: Police brutality
author: editorial
article_text:
The use of excessive force by police personnel remains a serious concern in Pakistan, where allegations of torture and abuse of authority continue to surface despite laws prohibiting such practices. The custodial death of Akmal Ali Khan, allegedly following an assault by policemen at a check-post in Taxila, calls for immediate accountability. The victim was reportedly beaten following a minor roadside dispute and later declared dead at a hospital. Three police personnel have been booked for murder. Such incidents are grave and must be investigated impartially, with those found responsible subjected to the full force of the law.

The persistence of police brutality reflects serious shortcomings in the country's law enforcement system. The police have long operated within a culture that tolerates coercion and intimidation, particularly when dealing with ordinary citizens who lack the means to challenge abuses of authority. Torture is frequently employed as a method of investigation or punishment, while officers accused of misconduct often escape criminal accountability. This has contributed to public distrust of the police and weakened the institution's ability to perform its fundamental duty of maintaining law and order.

Article 14 of the Constitution expressly prohibits torture for extracting evidence, while the Torture and Custodial Death (Prevention and Punishment) Act, 2022, provides a legal framework for prosecuting such offences. However, the implementation of these protections remains inadequate. FIA, which is empowered to investigate torture and custodial death cases, must be provided with the institutional independence necessary to fulfil its mandate. Investigations must be transparent and proceedings must be concluded without unnecessary delays. Departmental suspensions and transfers cannot be permitted to replace criminal prosecution. There is also an urgent need to strengthen the police system through comprehensive institutional reforms.

headline: Killer Karachi roads
description: Killer Karachi roads
author: editorial
article_text:
The authorities continue to fail as yet another heavy vehicle barrelling down Karachi's roads claims a precious life. Forty-five-year-old Faiza, who was pregnant, was riding pillion on a motorcycle driven by her husband, Fahim (55), when a speeding trailer hit them in Liaquatabad. Faiza succumbed to her injuries, and with her, her unborn child was also lost. Fahim remains under treatment for his injuries.

The ill-fated Faiza is not the first casualty of what has now become a hit-and-run culture in Karachi - driven by a host of factors, namely untrained drivers, excessive speeding, poor fleet maintenance, and, most critically, a total lack of regulatory oversight. Tragically, she will not be the last unless this fatal tendency to speed is acknowledged as a societal malady.

These heart-wrenching losses are part of a much wider, systemic crisis, as demonstrated by the staggering casualty numbers. In August 2025, a speeding dumper truck struck a motorcycle, killing siblings Mahnoor and Ahmed, while leaving their father critically injured. Another young man lost his life in December 2025 when a truck crashed into his motorcycle on the National Highway. Similarly, in January 2026, two seven-year-old boys were crushed to death in separate incidents – one by a water tanker and the other by a truck. It has been estimated that heavy vehicles claimed 147 lives in Karachi during the first six months of 2026.

While measures such as the Sindh government's daytime ban exist, they are not properly enforced. There must be rigid liability measures in place, such as revising Section 320 of the Pakistan Penal Code to make "causing death by rash or negligent driving" a non-bailable offence, which would compel drivers to be more vigilant. Additionally, installing GPS trackers and dashcams in commercial trucks would allow regulators to monitor speed and operating hours effectively. The daytime ban must also be strictly enforced through regular checks and increased police patrolling to prevent future violations.

Our roads must not become death traps. Enough lives have been lost. The carnage must stop now.

headline: Why can't I see my taxes working!
description: Do not tell me that taxes are necessary
author: Yumna Zahid Ali
article_text:
Every month, money is deducted from my salary in the name of taxes. I work for it, I earn it, and a portion of it goes to the government. Fine. But where are the results? If my money is being collected for the country's development, then why do the services my taxes pay for never seem to reach my own four walls? Is my money building a better Pakistan, or is it lining the pockets of a system that bleeds me dry and gives back scraps?

Why can't I see Karachi's public roads being properly developed? Why can't I see free, quality education for every child? Why can't I see clean drinking water reaching every household? Why can't I see a proper drainage system that prevents Karachi from turning into a swimming pool whenever it rains? Why can't I see footpaths that pedestrians can actually walk on instead of broken concrete, encroachments and open manholes? Why can't I see a public transport system that allows working-class commuters to get to work without being drained by the journey?

Why can't I see public schools with functioning toilets, clean classrooms, qualified teachers and proper furniture? Why can't I see government hospitals with enough beds, medical equipment and doctors who are not overwhelmed by endless queues? Why can't I see streetlights working in areas where women and children have to walk after sunset? Why can't I see a proper waste management system instead of garbage becoming a rotting fixture of residential streets?

And I could ask "why can't I see?" forever, but the better question is: why can't they see what they've done?

Why does being a citizen now come with a second bill for everything? I pay taxes, then pay school fees. I pay taxes, then pay hospital bills. I pay taxes, then pay for private transport because public transport is inadequate. I pay taxes, then pay for bottled water because clean drinking water cannot always be trusted. I pay taxes, then pay for private security because I am worried about safety. At this point, am I funding a government or running a parallel government out of my own pocket?

Taxes are not charity or donations. They are not money citizens hand over so officials can congratulate themselves on collecting revenue. Taxes are public money, and public money must serve the public.

Of course, running a country costs money. Nobody expects a country to be rebuilt in a week. But financial limitations are one thing; failing to show where public money goes, what progress has been made, and who answers when projects fail is another. If I am expected to pay taxes on time, I have every right to expect accountability on time.

I am not asking for gold-plated roads, private hospitals for every neighbourhood, or luxury facilities on every street. I am asking for what any taxpayer is owed. Clean water. Safe roads. Quality education. Accessible healthcare. Reliable transport. Proper sanitation. Public spaces that are maintained.

Do not tell me that taxes are necessary. I know they are. Tell me what they are achieving. Do not show me another announcement, another ribbon-cutting ceremony, or another development project on paper. Show me the road that has been repaired, the school that has been improved, the hospital that can treat patients, and the neighbourhood that finally has clean water.

A country cannot keep demanding financial sacrifice from its citizens while expecting them to remain satisfied with excuses. Patriotism does not mean switching off your brain, closing your eyes, and applauding every decision made in your name. Sometimes, patriotism means asking legitimate, justified and long-overdue questions because you want your country to function better.

But financial limitations are one thing; failing to show where public money goes, what progress has been made, and who answers when projects fail is another. If I am expected to pay taxes on time, I have every right to expect accountability on time.

I am not asking for gold-plated roads, private hospitals for every neighbourhood, or luxury facilities on every street. I am asking for what any taxpayer is owed. Clean water. Safe roads. Quality education. Accessible healthcare. Reliable transport. Proper sanitation. Public spaces that are maintained.

Do not tell me that taxes are necessary. I know they are. Tell me what they are achieving. Do not show me another announcement, another ribbon-cutting ceremony, or another development project on paper. Show me the road that has been repaired, the school that has been improved, the hospital that can treat patients, and the neighbourhood that finally has clean water.

A country cannot keep demanding financial sacrifice from its citizens while expecting them to remain satisfied with excuses. Patriotism does not mean switching off your brain, closing your eyes, and applauding every decision made in your name. Sometimes, patriotism means asking legitimate, justified and long-overdue questions because you want your country to function better.

headline: Need for a change in two postures
description: Need for a change in two postures
author: Majid Ehsan
article_text:
Pakistan faces two increasingly complex security challenges on its eastern and western borders. Both are characterised by hostility, mistrust and recurring confrontation, yet they differ fundamentally in their origins, character and strategic implications. India's increasingly assertive military posture and the Afghan Taliban's failure to restrain TTP call for a reassessment of Pakistan's responses. The question is not whether Pakistan possesses the strength and resolve to defend its interests, but how that strength can be exercised with prudence, confidence and clear political objectives.

The temptation to respond to belligerence with greater belligerence is understandable. However, relations between states cannot be reduced to the psychology of confronting a bully. Their behaviour is shaped by perceptions of power, domestic compulsions and national interests. A policy that succeeds in deterring one adversary may prove counterproductive against another. Pakistan must, therefore, avoid applying a common template to two distinctly different challenges.

On the eastern border, the May 2025 military confrontation altered prevailing assumptions about military coercion between Pakistan and India. Pakistan responded militarily before a ceasefire was reached on 10 May. Reuters reported? that the fighting represented the most serious confrontation between the nuclear armed neighbours in nearly three decades. The crisis demonstrated both the dangers of escalation and the continuing relevance of credible deterrence.

The strategic lesson of this short but very dangerous confrontation should not be confined to the military outcome. Pakistan demonstrated its willingness and capability to respond to aggression. Nevertheless, the larger challenge is translating that experience into sustainable deterrence and regional stability. India's decision to hold the IWT in abeyance introduced another dangerous dimension. In its award of 31 August 2026, the Court of Arbitration reaffirmed the treaty's continuing force and rejected unilateral abeyance as grounds for suspending obligations. India disputes the tribunal's jurisdiction. The controversy illustrates how political differences increasingly threaten the livelihoods and security of millions.

Pakistan needs a strong and proactive defensive posture towards India, but proactivity must not be confused with a preference for military confrontation. The purpose of deterrence is to prevent aggression, not perpetuate hostility. Military preparedness, diplomatic engagement and economic resilience must reinforce one another. Neither dialogue without credible deterrence nor deterrence without dialogue offers a satisfactory basis for lasting stability.

The western border presents a different predicament. Pakistan's expectations of a friendly government in Kabul following the Taliban's return in August 2021 have progressively given way to disappointment. The resurgence of the TTP and increasingly lethal attacks inside Pakistan have become central sources of friction. Islamabad protests the existence of terror sanctuaries, whereas Kabul consistently and knowingly denies all this. UNSC monitoring reports have repeatedly highlighted the TTP's presence in Afghanistan and its activities against Pakistan.

No state can remain indifferent to terrorist attacks launched from sanctuaries beyond its borders. Nevertheless, the central question is whether an increasingly aggressive military posture, accompanied by punitive measures, can persuade the Afghan Taliban to alter their behaviour. Military action may disrupt terrorist infrastructure and demonstrate resolve but unless it produces measurable changes in Kabul's conduct, its strategic value remains uncertain. Punitive action must not become a substitute for a clearly articulated political strategy. Recent border confrontations demonstrate how quickly hostility can acquire momentum of its own.

Pakistan must, therefore, distinguish between coercion as an instrument of policy and coercion as a policy in itself. Pressure on Kabul should pursue verifiable objectives, including denial of TTP sanctuaries, disruption of operational infrastructure and credible monitoring mechanisms. Military measures, where lawful and necessary, must remain proportionate. Diplomatic engagement, intelligence cooperation and calibrated economic measures should complement them.

The diplomatic door has not been entirely closed. During the Moscow Format consultations on 5 October 2026, Afghan Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi maintained that differences could be resolved through dialogue. Pakistan reiterated its demand for ending terrorist impunity on Afghan territory. The challenge is converting declarations into verifiable commitments.

Pakistan cannot afford indefinite confrontation on both borders. Sustained military readiness, disrupted trade and border closures impose considerable economic costs. Internal stability, economic recovery and institutional strength are indispensable elements of national security. A state perpetually responding to external provocations risks allowing adversaries to determine its strategic priorities.

Classical realism offers useful guidance. Hans J Morgenthau, in Politics Among Nations, regarded prudence – understood as weighing the political consequences of alternative courses of action – as the supreme virtue in politics. Prudence does not imply weakness or abandonment of national interests. Strength is indispensable, but without political judgment it can become a liability.

Pakistan's approach towards India and Afghanistan should rest on a common principle but follow different operational paths. With India, the priorities should be credible deterrence, strategic confidence, crisis management and meaningful political engagement. With Afghanistan, effective counterterrorism must be supported by diplomatic pressure, verifiable commitments and proportionate measures.

A bully's bluff may be called through a demonstration of resolve, but the underlying conflict is seldom resolved by humiliation. Tactical success may impose immediate costs; strategic success lies in creating conditions under which threats diminish, and recurring confrontation becomes less likely. Pakistan has both the right and responsibility to protect its sovereignty and citizens.

The need of the hour is neither appeasement nor unrestrained retaliation. It is a recalibration of the two postures, anchored in confidence, credible deterrence and prudence, while pursuing improvement through sustained dialogue. Ultimately, the true measure of national strength is not how severely an adversary can be punished, but how effectively a nation can safeguard its interests without becoming a prisoner of perpetual confrontation.

headline: GM seed governance - lessons from cotton
description: GM seed governance - lessons from cotton
author: News Desk
article_text:
Genetically modified (GM) seed technology has improved agricultural productivity, pest management and climate resilience globally. Bt cotton is a GM variety containing a gene from the soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) that protects against bollworms, reducing the need for insecticides. Pakistan formally commercialised Bt cotton in 2010 as its only widely adopted GM crop.

Yet despite Bt cotton accounting for an estimated 95% of the country's cotton area by 2022, national cotton production has fallen to a 40-year low. While many factors have contributed to this decline, including pests beyond Bt cotton's targeted bollworms, diseases such as Cotton Leaf Curl Virus, climate change and evolving crop economics; weaknesses in GM seed governance remain an important part of the story. This insight examines Pakistan's GM seed governance through the case of Bt cotton.

GM crops have been commercially cultivated since 1996 and, by 2025, were grown in 30 countries on 216 million hectares. GM cotton accounted for 76.7% of global cotton area, with Pakistan in fifth place. Yet large-scale adoption has not translated into sustained gains. India offers a useful regional comparison given similar adoption timelines and production systems.

India's cotton yield more than doubled from 191 kg/ha in 2002 to 440 kg/ha in 2024, reaching 511 kg/ha in 2016. Pakistan initially recorded a substantially higher yield of 622 kg/ha and peaked at 815 kg/ha in 2011, but subsequently experienced considerable volatility, falling to 390 kg/ha in 2022 before recovering to 590 kg/ha in 2024. Consequently, Pakistan's initial yield advantage over India narrowed substantially, suggesting that its early productivity streak was not sustained.

Bt cotton, based largely on Monsanto's first-generation Cry1Ac (MON531) technology, entered Pakistan informally around 2002, before effective systems for biosafety, variety registration and seed quality assurance were in place. By 2007, an estimated 60% of Pakistan's cotton area was already planted with unregulated Bt cotton. Despite formal commercialisation in 2010, regulatory oversight struggled to catch up with the established informal market. By 2012, 52 Bt varieties were being cultivated, but only nine were officially approved. Around 85% of seed samples had an unknown origin and only 1% met the required Bt toxin level.

Consequently, these factors increased Bt-targeted pest resistance and secondary pests, pushing farmers back towards pesticide use. Cotton area declined from 3.2 million hectares in 201415 to 1.9 million hectares by 2025, with pink bollworm alone estimated to cause annual losses of around one million bales. Furthermore, first-generation Cry1Ac technology remained widely used even as its effectiveness declined.

The experience also highlighted the importance of conserving cotton's genetic diversity. Studies found a narrow genetic base among cultivated varieties in Pakistan, while gene flow between Bt and non-Bt cotton was documented in Faisalabad. These findings raise concerns about cross-contamination and the long-term preservation of indigenous varieties and genetic resources essential for future breeding.

Pakistan has introduced a series of reforms to strengthen GM seed governance. Together, they provide a stronger institutional foundation than existed during the early years of Bt cotton adoption. However, important gaps remain.

The first gap is institutional coordination. GM crops must complete two separate regulatory processes: biosafety approval by the National Biosafety Committee (NBC) and seed certification and variety registration by the National Seed Development & Regulatory Authority (NSDRA). Yet, neither the Pakistan Biosafety Rules 2005 nor the Seed (Amendment) Act 2024 explicitly establishes a formal mechanism for coordination or information-sharing between the two authorities. A joint coordination mechanism could ensure that biosafety approval, seed certification and post-release oversight inform one another throughout a GM variety's lifecycle.

The second gap concerns post-release monitoring. While institutions such as the Pakistan Central Cotton Committee (PCCC) generate technical evidence, provincial agriculture departments are better placed to monitor crops in the field and identify local changes in crop performance and pest pressure. A formal linkage between provincial field monitoring, research institutions and NSDRA could ensure that such evidence informs national seed regulation and future approvals.

The third gap is research capacity. Sustained research and resistance monitoring are essential to maintaining GM crops' effectiveness. Globally, documented cases of practical resistance to Bt crops rose from three in 2005 to 16 by 2016. Pakistan's constrained agricultural research funding, including financial challenges at PCCC, underscores the need for stable funding for varietal evaluation, resistance monitoring and preservation of genetic diversity.

GM maize is the next test for Pakistan's seed governance. Maize covers 1.59 million hectares, with production estimated at 8.79 million tonnes in 202526. Unlike Bt cotton, which spread informally before effective regulation, GM maize is now being considered through a government-led commercialisation framework, with coexistence of GM and non-GM maize under discussion.

Safeguards should therefore be established before widespread adoption, including traceable seed, post-release monitoring and a clear biosafety framework. Designated cultivation zones, alongside appropriate isolation distances, could further limit cross-contamination between GM and non-GM maize, protecting non-GM production and preserving genetic diversity.

In conclusion, Pakistan's Bt cotton experience shows that technological adoption without strong governance can limit long-term gains. As GM agriculture expands, Pakistan must strengthen regulation, monitoring, research and stewardship before adoption outpaces oversight.
