Genetically modified (GM) seed technology has improved agricultural productivity, pest management and climate resilience globally. Bt cotton is a GM variety containing a gene from the soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) that protects against bollworms, reducing the need for insecticides. Pakistan formally commercialised Bt cotton in 2010 as its only widely adopted GM crop.

Yet despite Bt cotton accounting for an estimated 95% of the country's cotton area by 2022, national cotton production has fallen to a 40-year low. While many factors have contributed to this decline, including pests beyond Bt cotton's targeted bollworms, diseases such as Cotton Leaf Curl Virus, climate change and evolving crop economics; weaknesses in GM seed governance remain an important part of the story. This insight examines Pakistan's GM seed governance through the case of Bt cotton.

GM crops have been commercially cultivated since 1996 and, by 2025, were grown in 30 countries on 216 million hectares. GM cotton accounted for 76.7% of global cotton area, with Pakistan in fifth place. Yet large-scale adoption has not translated into sustained gains. India offers a useful regional comparison given similar adoption timelines and production systems.

India's cotton yield more than doubled from 191 kg/ha in 2002 to 440 kg/ha in 2024, reaching 511 kg/ha in 2016. Pakistan initially recorded a substantially higher yield of 622 kg/ha and peaked at 815 kg/ha in 2011, but subsequently experienced considerable volatility, falling to 390 kg/ha in 2022 before recovering to 590 kg/ha in 2024. Consequently, Pakistan's initial yield advantage over India narrowed substantially, suggesting that its early productivity streak was not sustained.

Bt cotton, based largely on Monsanto's first-generation Cry1Ac (MON531) technology, entered Pakistan informally around 2002, before effective systems for biosafety, variety registration and seed quality assurance were in place. By 2007, an estimated 60% of Pakistan's cotton area was already planted with unregulated Bt cotton. Despite formal commercialisation in 2010, regulatory oversight struggled to catch up with the established informal market. By 2012, 52 Bt varieties were being cultivated, but only nine were officially approved. Around 85% of seed samples had an unknown origin and only 1% met the required Bt toxin level.

Consequently, these factors increased Bt-targeted pest resistance and secondary pests, pushing farmers back towards pesticide use. Cotton area declined from 3.2 million hectares in 201415 to 1.9 million hectares by 2025, with pink bollworm alone estimated to cause annual losses of around one million bales. Furthermore, first-generation Cry1Ac technology remained widely used even as its effectiveness declined.

The experience also highlighted the importance of conserving cotton's genetic diversity. Studies found a narrow genetic base among cultivated varieties in Pakistan, while gene flow between Bt and non-Bt cotton was documented in Faisalabad. These findings raise concerns about cross-contamination and the long-term preservation of indigenous varieties and genetic resources essential for future breeding.

Pakistan has introduced a series of reforms to strengthen GM seed governance. Together, they provide a stronger institutional foundation than existed during the early years of Bt cotton adoption. However, important gaps remain.

The first gap is institutional coordination. GM crops must complete two separate regulatory processes: biosafety approval by the National Biosafety Committee (NBC) and seed certification and variety registration by the National Seed Development & Regulatory Authority (NSDRA). Yet, neither the Pakistan Biosafety Rules 2005 nor the Seed (Amendment) Act 2024 explicitly establishes a formal mechanism for coordination or information-sharing between the two authorities. A joint coordination mechanism could ensure that biosafety approval, seed certification and post-release oversight inform one another throughout a GM variety's lifecycle.

The second gap concerns post-release monitoring. While institutions such as the Pakistan Central Cotton Committee (PCCC) generate technical evidence, provincial agriculture departments are better placed to monitor crops in the field and identify local changes in crop performance and pest pressure. A formal linkage between provincial field monitoring, research institutions and NSDRA could ensure that such evidence informs national seed regulation and future approvals.

The third gap is research capacity. Sustained research and resistance monitoring are essential to maintaining GM crops' effectiveness. Globally, documented cases of practical resistance to Bt crops rose from three in 2005 to 16 by 2016. Pakistan's constrained agricultural research funding, including financial challenges at PCCC, underscores the need for stable funding for varietal evaluation, resistance monitoring and preservation of genetic diversity.

GM maize is the next test for Pakistan's seed governance. Maize covers 1.59 million hectares, with production estimated at 8.79 million tonnes in 202526. Unlike Bt cotton, which spread informally before effective regulation, GM maize is now being considered through a government-led commercialisation framework, with coexistence of GM and non-GM maize under discussion.

Safeguards should therefore be established before widespread adoption, including traceable seed, post-release monitoring and a clear biosafety framework. Designated cultivation zones, alongside appropriate isolation distances, could further limit cross-contamination between GM and non-GM maize, protecting non-GM production and preserving genetic diversity.

In conclusion, Pakistan's Bt cotton experience shows that technological adoption without strong governance can limit long-term gains. As GM agriculture expands, Pakistan must strengthen regulation, monitoring, research and stewardship before adoption outpaces oversight.

headline: The big show bows out: Maxwell retires from international cricket
description: Australian all-rounder folds 15-year international career but remains available for Melbourne Stars in Big Bash League
author: Sports Desk
article_text:
Australian all-rounder Glenn Maxwell on Monday night announced his retirement from international cricket, bringing an end to a career spanning more than a decade, while confirming he will continue playing in the Big Bash League (BBL). The 38-year-old has also retired from first-class and List A cricket but remains committed to the Melbourne Stars after extending his contract until the 2027-28 season. Maxwell had previously retired from one-day internationals in June 2025 but continued playing T20 internationals, representing Australia at the 2026 T20 World Cup. Australia's final match of that tournament, against Oman in February, proved to be his last international appearance. He took two wickets but did not get an opportunity to bat as Australia failed to progress beyond the group stage.

"A little bit sad and a little bit inevitable as well. Announcing my retirement from international cricket and domestic games for Victoria in the 50-over and four-day stuff. Red ball completely, probably won't shock anybody,” Maxwell said on the Final World Podcast. "After the last one-day game for Victoria, speaking to my teammates and letting them know that that was going to be my last game for the state was probably harder than I thought it was going to be. Knowing that they've played such a huge role in my whole career, every time I've come back, had great teammates there and a lot of support from the state,” said Maxwell. “Yeah, I certainly got a little bit choked up speaking in front of the group, but yeah, it's probably a time where I probably need to spend a little bit more time investing in the body to make sure I can get through the remaining couple of tournaments I've got in my career,” Maxwell said. "We probably had numerous discussions before and after the T20 World Cup," Maxwell said on the Final Word podcast, adding that the decision was made without pressure from the Australian team management. The two-time ODI World Cup winner said he had considered the possibility of playing a farewell international at the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG), but understood Australia's focus on rebuilding ahead of the 2028 Olympics. Maxwell played a key role in Australia's 2021 T20 World Cup triumph, scoring the winning runs in the final. He also became one of the most explosive batters in the shortest format, scoring 2,897 runs in 130 T20 internationals at a strike rate of 154.42. His tally includes five centuries, a joint world record in men's T20 internationals alongside India's Rohit Sharma. He also claimed 51 wickets in the format. Maxwell earned seven Test caps, scoring 339 runs, including a century against India in Ranchi in 2017. The all-rounder recently led Belfast Wolves to the final of the inaugural European T20 Premier League before representing Victoria in two One-Day Cup matches. Maxwell also revealed that managing his fitness had become a priority as he prepares for the remaining tournaments in his playing career. He had considered making himself available for Australia's upcoming white-ball series against England, which includes a T20 international in Melbourne, but opted to focus on recovering from a knee problem and preparing for the BBL. The Melbourne Stars will therefore remain his primary competitive commitment as he begins the next chapter of his cricket career.

"After the last one-day game for Victoria, speaking to my teammates and letting them know that that was going to be my last game for the state was probably harder than I thought it was going to be. Knowing that they've played such a huge role in my whole career, every time I've come back, had great teammates there and a lot of support from the state,” said Maxwell. “Yeah, I certainly got a little bit choked up speaking in front of the group, but yeah, it's probably a time where I probably need to spend a little bit more time investing in the body to make sure I can get through the remaining couple of tournaments I've got in my career,” Maxwell said. headline: Core inflation falls to 7.5% in Oct
description: Core inflation falls to 7.5% in Oct
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
The non-energy and non-food inflation eased for the second consecutive month to 7.5% in October, putting a question mark over the central bank's assumption that increasing energy and food prices may "seep into core inflation", which was used to raise its policy rate.

With the slowing pace, the difference between core inflation and the policy rate has substantially widened to 4.5% for the benefit of commercial banks, but at the expense of borrowers, mainly the finance ministry.

Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS) reported on Monday that the urban core inflation rate, calculated after excluding volatile energy and food prices, slowed down to 7.8% and rural inflation further fell to 7.1% in October. It was the second straight month when core inflation eased after peaking at 8.8% in August.

Core inflation gauges the underlying inflationary pressures without taking into account the highly volatile energy and food prices. The indicator was used as a base by the State Bank to increase the policy rate to 12% last week.

"There is a risk that elevated food and energy inflation may further increase inflation expectations, which may seep into core inflation going forward," said the monetary policy statement issued by the central bank after the policy rate decision.

The central bank noted that re-escalation in the Middle East conflict and domestic wheat supply frictions were the two major factors keeping inflation at elevated levels and their expected continuation over the next few months had worsened the inflation outlook.

It added that elevated prices of energy and wheat and its allied products contributed significantly to the headline inflation in September, which turned out to be higher than the Monetary Policy Committee's (MPC) expectation.

However, according to the PBS, the headline inflation slowed down to 9.6% last month, which was largely in line with the finance ministry's forecast for the month.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has raised Pakistan's inflation forecast to 9.9% for the current fiscal year, which is above the official target of 8.2% and is said to be a reason for the recent rate hike. The Planning Commission of Pakistan has projected a 7.5% inflation rate, even lower than the target.

According to the PBS, inflation went down both in urban and rural areas, reaching 9.5% in urban areas and 9.8% in rural areas. Food inflation slowed down from 8.1% to 7.8% in urban areas while it dropped to 7.1% in rural areas. The energy group saw a southbound movement in both urban and rural areas. The pace decelerated to 10.6% in urban areas and 12.1% in rural areas.

During review talks last month, the IMF asked Pakistan to adjust both exchange rate and interest rate policies to tame inflation and keep the current account deficit under check.

However, the cost of housing, water, electricity, gas and fuel remained the main concern in addition to transportation charges, according to the official bulletin.

PBS reported that petrol price was 42% higher in October compared to a year ago. Within one month, there was a 3% increase in prices of petrol, which was a steep rise given the overall high rates. The per-litre petrol cost was Rs379 on Friday last week and the price was Rs402 for high-speed diesel, which was keeping transport charges elevated.

The cost of transport services went up 27% last month compared to a year ago, according to the PBS. The national data collecting agency stated that electricity tariffs rose 23% in October. The high cost of electricity is already driving consumers away from the national power grid. Motor vehicle taxes jumped 39% over a year ago, contributing to the increase in expenses.

PBS said that onion prices were 82% higher year-on-year in October followed by a 39% increase in wheat prices. Owing to serious wheat management issues, the government is already in the process of importing 765,000 tonnes of wheat. Meanwhile, wheat flour prices surged 35% compared to a year ago, according to the PBS.

But prices of tomatoes, potatoes, sugar, eggs and pulses were lower in the range of 55% to 10% last month. The closure of border with Afghanistan and the subsequent suspension of trade have helped keep prices low for these commodities, which are either exported or smuggled, but contributed to an increase in prices of fruits that were imported from the western neighbour.

headline: Oil falls 7.5% on peace hopes, gold up
description: Oil falls 7.5% on peace hopes, gold up
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
Oil prices fell more than 7% on Monday as talks between Iranian and Qatari officials lifted hopes for an end to the US-Israel war with Iran and stabilisation of Middle East crude supply.

Iran's president said the supreme leader had granted the government "certain authorities" regarding peace talks. The country's negotiators held days of talks with Qatari mediators aimed at ending the war. A draft proposal is being circulated, with a follow-up meeting possible, an official briefed on the talks said.

Brent crude futures fell $8.47, or 7.47%, to $104.96 a barrel by 1724 GMT, as per Reuters. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude was down $7.50, or 7.2%, at $96.62. The session low for Brent was $104.49 and for WTI, it was $96.44, with analysts citing hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough.

Signs of progress in US-Iran talks pushed oil prices lower, Raymond James' analyst Pavel Molchanov said, noting, however, that scepticism was warranted after many "false dawns" over the past several months.

Meanwhile, gold prices in Pakistan rebounded on Monday, gaining Rs2,400 per tola to Rs412,136, tracking recovery in the international market, as easing oil prices helped temper inflation concerns. In the international market, spot gold rose 2.1% to $3,957.19 per ounce by 1411 GMT, recovering from a one-year low hit in the previous session. US gold futures for December delivery advanced 1.77% to $3,967.40.

According to rates released by the All-Pakistan Gems and Jewellers Sarafa Association, the price of 10-gram gold increased Rs2,058 to Rs353,340. On Saturday, gold had plunged Rs10,800 per tola to Rs409,736, reflecting a sharp decline in international bullion rates.

The international recovery came as oil prices fell more than 7% on Monday following a third consecutive day of talks between Iranian and Qatari officials aimed at ending the US-Israel war with Iran. Lower oil prices eased concerns about inflationary pressures, providing some support to precious metals.

Peter Grant, Vice President and Senior Metals Strategist at Zaner Metals, noted that markets were still anticipating a US Federal Reserve rate hike in December, although expectations had eased slightly. Traders were pricing in a 77% probability of a rate hike, down from 80% a week earlier, according to CME Group's FedWatch Tool.

Furthermore, the Pakistani rupee appreciated Rs0.03 against the US dollar to close at Rs276.72 in the inter-bank market, extending its marginal gains.

headline: Eurobond debt may be tokenised
description: Eurobond debt may be tokenised
author: APP
article_text:
The Ministry of Finance and the government are reviewing the possibility of tokenising Pakistan's existing Eurobond debt, Federal Minister for Finance and Revenue Senator Muhammad Aurangzeb said, as he pressed banks to adopt digital assets responsibly while keeping restrictions on their own holdings of virtual assets.

Addressing a dialogue on digital assets and the future of banking organised by the Pakistan Banks' Association and LUMS, he said financial innovation should deliver lower-cost remittances, faster business payments, accessible financing for entrepreneurs and increased productive investment.

"Pakistan needs financial innovation, and digital assets must complement the broader digital transformation," he said.

He said digital transformation must be accompanied by strong regulatory safeguards, financial stability and institutional oversight so that technological advancement did not create unnecessary risks.

He said the government had achieved macroeconomic stability and was now focused on export-led growth through economic discipline, higher exports, foreign direct investment and private-sector participation.

He also said banks needed to facilitate businesses, particularly small and medium enterprises and agriculture, through easier access to financing.

Pakistan established a statutory framework through the Virtual Assets Act 2026, assigning the Pakistan Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority responsibility for licensing and supervising virtual asset service providers.

He said the next priority was effective implementation through capable supervision and institutional coordination.

The State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) has introduced a conditional mechanism for extending banking facilities to licensed entities, subject to due diligence and segregation of client funds.

The minister said accounts opened for entities holding no-objection certificates would serve a limited purpose until licensing was complete, and that banks remained responsible for foreign exchange compliance.

He said restrictions on banks investing, trading or holding virtual assets through their own funds or customer deposits would remain.

Aurangzeb said tokenisation could improve remittance channels, including transactions linked to Roshan Digital Accounts.

Pakistan received $41.6 billion in remittances last fiscal year, and first-quarter trends suggest inflows could exceed $44 billion.

headline: Pakistan's quiet resilience in first quarter of FY27
description: Pakistan's quiet resilience in first quarter of FY27
author: News Desk
article_text:
Let's be honest: the past few months have been hard on almost everyone. Conflict in the Middle East disrupted oil and gas supplies, energy prices climbed, and even major economies struggled to keep their balance. So how did Pakistan fare? For a country that imports most of its energy and has long battled foreign currency shortages, July to September 2026 was a serious test.

The answer may surprise you. Pakistan didn't just hold its ground; it moved forward. The latest economic scorecard reflects steady policy under Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's government, close coordination with the military leadership under Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, and an economic team led by Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb that kept reforms on course. Above all, it reflects the hard work of ordinary Pakistanis.

Start with the number that matters most in a crisis. The State Bank's foreign exchange reserves reached $21.5 billion, an all-time high, up 52% in a year. This safety net has kept the rupee stable, even gaining 1.5%, and keeps fuel, medicine and other essential imports flowing. Import cover has risen from 2.2 to 3.3 months, a vital breathing room in turbulent times.

Pakistan's earners didn't slow down either. Exports grew 11% to $11.2 billion, with September's goods exports the highest in 20 months. Technology stood out: IT exports rose 18% to $1.25 billion, and freelancers earned a record $550 million, up 46%. Picture a young developer in Multan or a designer in Peshawar winning clients in London and Dubai from a laptop.

Overseas Pakistanis once again showed how much home means to them. Remittances rose 14% to $10.9 billion, mainly from Saudi Arabia, the UAE, the UK and the EU, while the Roshan Digital Account has drawn $14.3 billion across nearly 976,000 accounts. That confidence is spreading. Foreign direct investment rose 20% to $720 million while investors worldwide held back. All three major rating agencies have upgraded Pakistan into the 'B' category with stable outlooks, rewarding the fiscal discipline and steady engagement with lenders central to Finance Minister Aurangzeb's approach. The IMF programme is firmly on track, with a staff-level agreement reached for $1.2 billion.

Pakistanis at home are investing too. Stock market investors jumped 55% to over 656,000, and 85% of new investors are Gen-Z and Millennials. Four companies listed this quarter, raising Rs4.6 billion, roughly five times last year's total.

Pakistan's voice abroad is growing as well. On November 1, Pakistan became chair of the G-24, the bloc of developing countries founded in 1971 to coordinate positions on global finance. Finance Minister Aurangzeb, who will lead it, put it powerfully: "The future of developing economies is not peripheral to the future of the global economy. It is central to it." Pakistan will push for affordable development financing, fairer debt solutions and climate resilience. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called it a "significant diplomatic milestone", and President Asif Ali Zardari termed it an important opportunity to represent the developing world.

What does this mean for businesses and jobs? The policy rate, which hit 22% in June 2024, now stands at 12%, and cheaper money is flowing. Loans to small and medium businesses rose 66% to Rs1.14 trillion, housing finance grew 72%, and lending to farmers and auto buyers rose roughly 31% and 34%. That means shops opening, homes built, harvests financed and jobs created.

The country is also learning to stand on its own feet. The FBR collected Rs3.1 trillion in three months, beating its target, while income tax filers jumped 45% to 5.77 million, reflecting the tax reforms and digitisation championed by the finance ministry. Government debt has fallen to 68% of GDP from 75% in FY23.

Momentum is visible on the ground too. Car sales rose 28%, cement and petroleum sales grew, and large-scale manufacturing is expanding. Privatisation of power distribution companies – Fesco, Gepco and Iesco – is advancing, drawing local and foreign interest. And when fuel prices rose, a Rs75 billion relief scheme reached more than 12 million citizens who depend on motorcycles, rickshaws and small cars.

Is the job done? Not yet. Global events have pushed up prices at home, many families still feel the squeeze, and sustaining reforms will require patience. But stronger reserves, a wider tax base, lower debt and returning investor confidence are the foundation for what people need: stronger support for low-income families, new schools, hospitals and roads, and, over time, real relief from the cost of living.

This achievement belongs to everyone who made it possible: the worker and the farmer, the young freelancer, the overseas Pakistani sending money home, and a leadership and economic team that held their nerve through a turbulent quarter.

The writer Jamella Zarif is an Islamabad-based investigative journalist.

headline: Agri-output as vital as industrial productivity
description: Agri-output as vital as industrial productivity
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
Agricultural productivity holds equal importance to industrial productivity given its contribution to food security, employment and raw material supply to industry, National Productivity Organisation (NPO) Chief Executive Officer Muhammad Alamgir Chaudhry said as a five-day international workshop on smart agriculture opened in Lahore and the Asian Productivity Organisation (APO) National Productivity Awards 2025 were presented.

He said smart agriculture, sustainable soil management, resource-efficient production and innovative value-added solutions could improve agricultural performance, strengthen agriculture-industry linkages and create new opportunities for agro-based enterprises.

The workshop, running from November 2 to 6, 2026, will focus on sustainable soil management, data-driven farming, product quality and value addition, according to a statement issued on Monday.

Joint Secretary at the Ministry of Industries and Production Nadeemur Rehman, the chief guest, said agriculture remained a cornerstone of the economy and called for transforming traditional practices through sustainable soil management, efficient resource use, modern technology and value addition.

He linked farm modernisation to economic transformation objectives under URAAN Pakistan and the 5Es National Economic Transformation Plan, and appreciated APO's technical support across its member economies.

The APO National Productivity Awards 2025 were presented at the opening ceremony for achievement in productivity improvement, innovation, operational excellence and promoting a productivity-driven culture in Pakistan.

headline: 'Closed for debt but open for business in equity'
description: 'Closed for debt but open for business in equity'
author: Shahbaz Rana
article_text:
Bangladesh's Finance Adviser to the Prime Minister, Dr Rashid Al Mehmood Titumir, on Monday proposed a five-point development paradigm for South Asia to deal with disruptive geopolitical challenges, emphasising that legitimacy matters for becoming a welfare state.

In his keynote speech at the annual Sustainable Development Policy Conference, Titumir said regional countries needed to reconstruct the fiscal state, reposition industrial policies and build multilateral cooperation.

He said there was a need to rethink conventional fiscal consolidation, whose purpose should be to preserve the state's capacity to invest in the future, not simply to minimise public expenditure.

Pakistan's Climate Change Minister Dr Musadiq Malik shared those concerns, saying debt-driven growth was unacceptable as servicing was eating half the country's revenues.

"I would propose that we could come up with a South Asian framing of a new development paradigm," with at least five strategic priorities, Titumir said.

He proposed moving from efficiency-driven development to resilience-oriented development, saying recent crises showed that efficiency without resilience creates significant vulnerabilities.

Titumir also proposed repositioning industrial policy as an instrument of structural transformation, saying the challenge was no longer simply to attract investment. "It is to attract investment that builds domestic capabilities, generates employment, transfers technology, and strengthens linkages with the wider economy," he said.

He called for a production network where South Asia, Southeast Asia and the Middle East and North Africa work together across primary, intermediate and finished goods, while remaining mindful of an active industrial policy.

He suggested reconstructing the fiscal state and rethinking development financing, saying the state's capacity to mobilise and allocate resources was becoming a critical determinant of national resilience. Developing countries, he said, needed stronger domestic revenue mobilisation, more efficient spending, modernised public financial management and more sophisticated capital markets.

His fourth proposal placed human capabilities and employment at the centre of economic transformation. Fifth, he also stressed multilateral cooperation, saying no country, irrespective of economic or military strength, can independently resolve challenges such as climate change, pandemics, financial instability, technological governance, international taxation and maritime security.

Sharing Bangladesh's experience, the finance adviser said "the foremost lesson that we have learned in Bangladesh, if we are to say it in a single sentence, is that legitimacy matters."

"Legitimacy must originate from the people. So what we are trying to do is come up with a prime ministerial vision of a Bangladesh which is democratic, which is humane, and which has a welfare state," he said.

Dr Malik criticised the debt-led model, noting that money for the poor had decreased by 23% in a year. "The money that was available for development in 2015, when the SDGs started, is where we have fallen back to in one year," he said.

"We collect Rs16 trillion, of which roughly Rs8 trillion is paid in debt servicing. That is about 48% of our revenue. When shall we stop? This kind of development at the expense of our future is unacceptable."

Malik is the second cabinet minister after Ahsan Iqbal to speak against debt-led growth. The planning minister has described Pakistan's stabilisation as "stunted and borrowed."

Malik said Pakistan was willing to do development for debt swaps and open for business in equity. "We're not open for more debts. That shop is closed."

But contrary to that claim, the finance ministry is taking a $500 million foreign loan to bring local employees into a contributory pension scheme and a $600 million loan whose conditions include amending a simple import order and allowing the private sector to import urea.

Titumir said the world was not simply experiencing another episode of uncertainty but a structural transformation of the international economic and political order, with the institutions and models that shaped the post-war system challenged simultaneously and the boundaries between economics and geopolitics, technology and security, climate and development blurring.

For developing countries these disruptions are consequential and not merely external shocks to be absorbed, he said. He listed 10 disruptive forces, including the international political and economic order, trade and production networks, technology, climate change, debt, growth and distribution, institutional disruptions, information and trust, and demography.

A young population without adequate education, skills and employment can become a source of frustration but, with the right framework, a major source of productivity, innovation and domestic demand, he said.

He said investment should go into production, which would generate decent employment and could finance the social sector.

headline: PSX records thin gains in volatile session
description: PSX records thin gains in volatile session
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) staged a late recovery on Monday to close marginally higher, reversing an earlier decline as investors weighed hopes of diplomatic progress in the Middle East against selling pressure across key sectors.

The benchmark KSE-100 index edged higher by 154.81 points, or 0.09%, to settle at 166,564.07, after remaining under pressure for much of the session. In the morning, the market opened on a cautious note, with selling emerging soon and the index slipping to 166,169.41 at 9:34 am, down 239.84 points, or 0.14%.

The selling pressure deepened during the day, pulling the index down to 165,776.85 at 12:29 pm, down 632.40 points, or 0.38%. However, the market subsequently recovered, where the benchmark touched the intra-day high of 166,989.76 and settled in positive territory. The market's positive close came amid a more than 4% decline in global oil prices as renewed hopes of diplomatic progress on ending the US-Israel war with Iran eased concerns over energy costs and pressure on Pakistan's import bill.

According to Arif Habib Limited (AHL), the PSX made a flat start to the week with the KSE-100 trading on both positive and negative sides. Some 41 shares rose while 58 fell with Mari Energies (+3.15%), Fauji Fertiliser (+0.92%) and Engro Holdings (+1.57%) contributing the most to the index's gains. Conversely, Attock Refinery (-10%), OGDC (-1.66%) and PSO (-2.33%) were the biggest index drags.

All refineries hit their lower limits as the government shifted the impact of higher petrol import costs onto local refineries to avoid passing it on to consumers. The ex-refinery motor spirit (MS) price rose Rs15.13 to Rs282.26 per litre, but it was offset by a reduction of Rs14.71 in the petroleum levy and a reduction of Rs0.42 in the inland freight equalisation margin (IFEM), leaving the ex-depot price unchanged at Rs377.91 per litre.

headline: Mineral incentive package on cards
description: Mineral incentive package on cards
author: ZAFAR BHUTTA
article_text:
The government is set to announce an incentive package to tap the full potential of copper and gold reserves, estimated at $8 trillion, in the National Mineral Policy – 2026. A model of the package, drawn up by Wood Mackenzie, has incorporated reduced withholding tax rates on local goods and services – 4% for local goods and 8% for local services – together with deferral until mine production.

The incentive package had been submitted to the Finance Division during the current year's budget but the inability to introduce a comprehensive programme at that time reflects major challenges in the way of finalising an investment-oriented National Mineral Policy. The government plans to offer these incentives to foreign investors during the upcoming Mineral Forum scheduled for November 12-13.

The prime minister had directed the Petroleum Division to develop and finalise the National Mineral Policy. However, sources said the policy document was ready but without a corresponding fiscal package it may not achieve the desired objectives and address the key challenges facing the mineral sector.

The Finance Division is the authority that can approve these fiscal packages, therefore the Petroleum Division has requested it to accord due importance and priority to the proposals and facilitate their early approval. These measures may be announced at the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum (PMIF).

Sources told The Express Tribune that there was a proposal to grant a 30-year exemption from general sales tax (GST) on the import and local purchase and supply of goods and services for mining projects during the exploration and development phase until the commencement of commercial production.

Another proposal says the exemption may continue after the commencement of production, particularly considering the fact that a substantial proportion of mineral production is export-oriented and input sales tax may remain unadjusted. Furthermore, it is proposed that the withholding tax applicable to contractors and suppliers for mining projects may be reduced during the exploration and development phase and payment/deposit of such taxes may be deferred until the commencement of commercial production.

The government has proposed that import duties on capital goods and project-related equipment for mining companies may be exempted during the exploration, development and construction phases. The Wood Mackenzie model treats customs/import duty exemption as an important component of the fiscal package.

A major proposal is to replace the conventional corporate income tax with a 1% presumptive tax on export proceeds together with a 0.5% development surcharge, aimed at providing a simple and predictable fiscal framework while encouraging investment. The Wood Mackenzie analysis identifies corporate income tax treatment as the single largest driver of improvement in an investor's internal rate of return (IRR).

Stability of fiscal regime

The consultancy firm has proposed that appropriate fiscal stability clauses be incorporated to protect the fiscal terms applicable at the time of award of an exploration concession/agreement, broadly along the lines of the stability framework available to the oil and gas sector. Fiscal stability is particularly important for mining because project development can span several years and investment decisions are made against long-term assumptions regarding taxation and government take.

It has suggested that mining projects may be exempted from super tax for at least 30 years to improve project economics and maintain competitiveness with other mineral-producing jurisdictions. Also, the withholding tax on dividends distributed by mining projects may be exempted for 15 years from commercial production. Inter-corporate dividends within mining project structures are also proposed to be exempted to avoid tax cascading within project structures.

Exploration losses

The consultancy firm proposes that exploration losses may be carried forward perpetually for mining projects, recognising that exploration expenditure can precede commercial production by several years and may also be incurred on unsuccessful exploration programmes. Additionally, losses from failed exploration projects may be adjusted against successful mining projects within the same mining group, subject to appropriate safeguards.

It suggests that carry-forward depreciation allowance for mining projects may be allowed for 10 years after the commencement of commercial production. Apart from that, accelerated depreciation up to 100% may be permitted for mining projects.

In its model, Wood Mackenzie has highlighted a 10-year carry-forward for the depreciation allowance together with 100% accelerated depreciation, by increasing the standard depreciation rate from 15% to 30%. It proposes that the fiscal regime applicable to mining projects may, where appropriate, be aligned with the special fiscal framework available to the oil and gas sector under the Fifth Schedule of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, recognising similarities in terms of exploration risk, capital intensity, long gestation periods and the need for fiscal stability.

headline: AI puts hourly billing model at risk
description: AI puts hourly billing model at risk
author: Usman Hanif
article_text:
Pakistan's information technology (IT) exporters must shift from low-margin, hourly outsourcing to high-value, outcome-based work as artificial intelligence (AI) commoditises conventional coding and manual quality assurance, industry experts said, with software exports and consultancy accounting for 41% of the country's IT exports and generating a combined $521 million in foreign exchange during the first quarter of the current financial year.

Continuing to bill by the hour will shrink revenues as AI tools boost developer efficiency, and firms should move to value-based pricing while building proprietary software accelerators and micro-IP, they said, warning that local companies face growing pressure to adopt AI and to address a shortage of skilled human resources.

According to data released by the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP), software consultancy generated $364 million in export receipts during July to September FY27, while software exports contributed $157 million. In the corresponding period last year, the two segments earned $293 million and $143 million respectively, a combined year-on-year increase of around 19%, or $85 million.

ClearTraced Co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Abdullah Rashid, whose company is a Sweden-based AI data firm, said Pakistani IT companies could expand their export business by developing expertise in specific industries and building AI solutions around customers' operational needs. A system that extracts information from company reports, for example, should show where each figure came from and allow users to identify and correct errors, he said, adding that getting details such as the reporting year and measurement units right is essential if the information is to support business decisions.

Firms must move up the software value chain by building specialised capability in enterprise AI integration, autonomous agentic workflows, data engineering and cybersecurity, he said. Rather than offering basic web or app development, they should position themselves as domain-specific technical partners for industries such as fintech, healthcare and logistics.

Workforce structure must also evolve from large teams of junior coders to lean teams of AI-augmented solution architects, he said, with exporters systematically upskilling developers on AI-assisted workflows and international compliance standards such as SOC 2 and the General Data Protection Regulation to win enterprise trust.

Market diversification is critical as well, he said. Beyond the United States and the United Kingdom, Pakistani firms must establish a physical sales presence in high-growth regions such as the Gulf Cooperation Council, particularly Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, where large digital transformation budgets are seeking cost-effective, specialised AI implementation partners.

He said firms could build longer-term export relationships by taking responsibility for integrating systems into customers' existing operations and maintaining them after deployment, and that understanding the customer's industry, handling data responsibly and demonstrating measurable improvements would help them compete for more valuable work.

He added that Pakistani firms have room to expand into higher-value projects in Europe and other developed markets, and that partnerships with international companies, participation in trade fairs and stronger engagement by trade attachés could help local businesses reach prospective customers and understand their requirements.

According to SBP data, Pakistan's IT exports, including computer services and related activities, exceeded $1.2 billion in the first quarter of FY27. During the period, IT freelancers generated $333 million in export receipts, while call centres contributed $101 million and telecommunications services earned more than $75 million.

Hexalyze Chief Executive Officer Saad Shah said faster AI adoption in Pakistan would depend on equipping the workforce with skills aligned with emerging industry requirements, and called for regular updates to technology curricula at universities and colleges alongside stronger in-house training and capacity-building programmes within IT companies.

He also acknowledged government and non-governmental initiatives aimed at training IT professionals and students but stressed the need for closer collaboration between industry and academia and a long-term roadmap for workforce development, saying sustained investment in skills would help local companies adapt to technological change, improve competitiveness and capture emerging opportunities in international markets.

The experts said Pakistan should also use its growing international engagement to promote locally developed technology products and services, helping domestic IT companies move beyond conventional outsourcing towards higher-value exports.

headline: 220kV transmission line energised
description: 220kV transmission line energised
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
For the youth of Sindh, this provides a chance to build career close to home

NationalGrid-Pakistan has energised a 220-kilovolt (kV) transmission line from Jhimpir-II to the Dhabeji sub-station, paving the way for reliable electricity supply to the Dhabeji Special Economic Zone (SEZ) and for new jobs, investment and growth in the region.

Completed at a cost of Rs1,806.90 million, the project is in line with the federal government's decision to develop the Dhabeji SEZ as a centre of industrial activity since dependable power will keep factories running, businesses investing and families earning.

As industries are set up and expanded in the zone, these businesses are expected to create livelihoods for local communities, strengthen supply chains and contribute to the national economy. For the youth of Sindh, this provides a chance to build career close to home. NationalGrid MD Engineer Altaf Hussain Malik remarked, "it is an important step towards strengthening the power infrastructure serving the Dhabeji SEZ and supporting its long-term industrial development objectives."

headline: Karachi festival offers a cultural feast
description: Karachi festival offers a cultural feast
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
The fifth day of the 3rd World Culture Festival at the Arts Council of Pakistan, Karachi, featured a vibrant mix of art, music, dance, film and theatre, bringing together international artists to celebrate cultural diversity and creative expression.

As part of its 'Artfelt: Conversations Series', the festival hosted a panel discussion titled 'Cultural Diversity as Represented in 21st Century Fine Art', featuring artists from Ethiopia, Germany, Singapore, Sweden and Kenya.

Participants Kaleab Alemayehu, Petra Kaltenbach, Yip Yew Chong, Domi Forest and Nelson Ijaka discussed contemporary art, artificial intelligence (AI) and the role of artistic expression in promoting cultural identity and understanding.

Alemayehu said art could transcend political divisions and connect people, while Kaltenbach emphasised dialogue and self-transformation as tools for positive change. Yip spoke about using his artwork to introduce Pakistan's beauty to audiences abroad, while Forest called for greater love and solidarity. Ijaka described art as a means of shaping cultural narratives and building national pride.

The festival also featured a music workshop, 'Beyond the Bassline', by Japanese guitarist Juna Serita, who demonstrated the bass guitar's potential as a lead instrument and introduced young musicians to improvisation techniques. Brazilian dance group Cia Livre De Danca Da Rocinha conducted a workshop on traditional Brazilian and Samba styles, while an open mic session showcased young singers.

Eight films were screened under the 'Arab and North African Shorts' programme, exploring themes including Palestinian identity, displacement, memory, family struggles, social injustice and psychological conflict.

The theatre programme featured Italian performer Tom Corradini's 50-minute physical comedy 'Shaolin Clown', which explored self-discovery through movement and humour. Pakistani production 'Taleem-e-Balighan', written and directed by Farhan Alam Siddiqui, offered a satirical take on social decline through the chaotic encounters of students at an adult education centre. Both productions received an enthusiastic response, bringing the festival's fifth day to a lively close.

headline: Changing fortunes of India's royals
description: Changing fortunes of India's royals
author: AFP
article_text:
In a sprawling palace in western India, the "queen" or Maharani of Baroda welcomes guests with fragrant rose petals, presenting torchlit dances of Hindu myths.

Dressed in glittering finery, Radhikaraje Gaekwad is a queen in name only, a modern businesswoman presiding over a world her ancestors once ruled.

"The key has been that we have adapted," 48-year-old Gaekwad told AFP in her vast Lakshmi Vilas Palace, describing how India's former royals have found new roles, from cultural ambassadors to politics.

"My work has always been to try and bring in change for what I feel would be for the betterment of society," said Gaekwad, who works to preserve art accumulated by generations of rulers. "A glimpse of what was left behind... can bring that sense of identity and pride back in their roots, and help them in the future."

Under British rule, more than 565 princely states enjoyed nominal autonomy across roughly 40% of the land. Baroda, today Vadodara in Gujarat state, was among the most powerful.

The maharajas joined democratic India after independence in 1947 and became ordinary citizens, but their enduring cultural influence is something politicians of all parties seek to harness.

"This cultural capital has been banked on by the descendants of the erstwhile maharajas to get into active politics," said historian Manu S Pillai.

Quest for heroes

Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu-nationalist government has sought to draw on a royal past outside foreign control to reinforce its national narrative. Modi's party includes elected lawmakers such as Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia, of the Gwalior dynasty, and Rajasthan Deputy Chief Minister Diya Kumari, of Jaipur's royal family.

"There is a quest for heroes," Pillai added. "Nationalist history has become very popular and... the Hindu right is very keen to tap into cultural icons."

Modi last year laid the foundation stone for a $39 million "Museum of Royal Kingdoms" celebrating their history. The site near Vadodara lies beside the world's tallest statue, a 182-metre monument to Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, whom Modi honoured with its inauguration in 2018 for his role in bringing princely states into India.

Visitors were divided over the role of royals today. "I hold the royal families in high regard," said Arti Shukla, visiting from Vadodara. Nishant Kulkarni, a bank worker from Mumbai, was more cynical. "I only came to see this massive statue," he said. "The royal families certainly played a role in the past, but there is no real need for their services anymore."

Storytellers

Beyond politics, many maharajahs see themselves as stewards of tradition, said Siddhaant Mohta, director of Sopaan, which organises cultural exhibitions in royal sitesincluding in Vadodara's palace. "The royal families are custodians of heritage," Mohta said, pointing to work to overhaul Vadodara's Maharaja Fateh Singh Museum, which houses more than 30 works by celebrated 19th-century painter Raja Ravi Varma.

A Varma work fetched $17.9 million at auction in Mumbai in April, an Indian record.

Deborah Swallow, former director of London's Courtauld Institute of Art, is advising on the project, praising the legacy of royal patronage that helped fund it. "That tradition is being beautifully followed today," she said.

Others, such as Raseshwari Rajya Laxmi, Maharani of Jaisalmer, said their titles open doorsexplaining how her family has helped twin the historic walled city with Carcassonne in France. "We are sharing ideas on promoting and preserving their culture," she said.

For Gaekwad, her work includes social entrepreneurship, promoting social inclusion through initiatives such as a transgender-run cafe, as well as supporting traditional crafts and customs.

Her father, Ranjitsinh Jhala, 87, took a different path. Born into Wankaner's ruling family in 1939, before India's princes surrendered their powers, he was raised in a world where tiger hunting was a royal passion.

But he became a civil servant, drafted India's wildlife protection law, and helped turn vast tracts of princely hunting grounds into national parks. "If that was what the princes left behind, it compensates far more than what they shot," he said.

Akshita Bhanj Deo, in her 30s, daughter of the 47th ruler of Odisha's Bhanja dynasty, represents a younger generation seeking modern meaning in historic titles. She has turned her palace into a hotel, and runs a foundation to support marginalised groups.

"A lot of erstwhile royal families see themselves in a space where they can actually make a sense of community happen," she said. "We're just the bards and storytellers between the past and future."

"This cultural capital has been banked on by the descendants of the erstwhile maharajas to get into active politics," said historian Manu S Pillai.
Quest for heroes

Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu-nationalist government has sought to draw on a royal past outside foreign control to reinforce its national narrative. Modi's party includes elected lawmakers such as Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia, of the Gwalior dynasty, and Rajasthan Deputy Chief Minister Diya Kumari, of Jaipur's royal family.
"There is a quest for heroes," Pillai added. "Nationalist history has become very popular and... the Hindu right is very keen to tap into cultural icons."

Modi last year laid the foundation stone for a $39 million "Museum of Royal Kingdoms" celebrating their history. The site near Vadodara lies beside the world's tallest statue, a 182-metre monument to Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, whom Modi honoured with its inauguration in 2018 for his role in bringing princely states into India.

Visitors were divided over the role of royals today. "I hold the royal families in high regard," said Arti Shukla, visiting from Vadodara. Nishant Kulkarni, a bank worker from Mumbai, was more cynical. "I only came to see this massive statue," he said. "The royal families certainly played a role in the past, but there is no real need for their services anymore."
Storytellers

Beyond politics, many maharajahs see themselves as stewards of tradition, said Siddhaant Mohta, director of Sopaan, which organises cultural exhibitions in royal sitesincluding in Vadodara's palace. "The royal families are custodians of heritage," Mohta said, pointing to work to overhaul Vadodara's Maharaja Fateh Singh Museum, which houses more than 30 works by celebrated 19th-century painter Raja Ravi Varma.
A Varma work fetched $17.9 million at auction in Mumbai in April, an Indian record.

Deborah Swallow, former director of London's Courtauld Institute of Art, is advising on the project, praising the legacy of royal patronage that helped fund it. "That tradition is being beautifully followed today," she said.

Others, such as Raseshwari Rajya Laxmi, Maharani of Jaisalmer, said their titles open doorsexplaining how her family has helped twin the historic walled city with Carcassonne in France. "We are sharing ideas on promoting and preserving their culture," she said.
For Gaekwad, her work includes social entrepreneurship, promoting social inclusion through initiatives such as a transgender-run cafe, as well as supporting traditional crafts and customs.

Her father, Ranjitsinh Jhala, 87, took a different path. Born into Wankaner's ruling family in 1939, before India's princes surrendered their powers, he was raised in a world where tiger hunting was a royal passion.

But he became a civil servant, drafted India's wildlife protection law, and helped turn vast tracts of princely hunting grounds into national parks. "If that was what the princes left behind, it compensates far more than what they shot," he said.

Akshita Bhanj Deo, in her 30s, daughter of the 47th ruler of Odisha's Bhanja dynasty, represents a younger generation seeking modern meaning in historic titles. She has turned her palace into a hotel, and runs a foundation to support marginalised groups.
"A lot of erstwhile royal families see themselves in a space where they can actually make a sense of community happen," she said. "We're just the bards and storytellers between the past and future."

headline: Ritchie expands 'The Gentlemen' universe
description: Ritchie expands 'The Gentlemen' universe
author: News Desk
article_text:
Netflix's crime drama 'The Gentlemen' is returning for a third season, with Robert Carlyle, Elijah Wood and Orlando Bloom among the new additions to its expanding cast as production gets under way in the United Kingdom and Morocco.

Created by Guy Ritchie, the series will see Theo James reprise his role as Eddie Horniman, alongside Kaya Scodelario as Susie Glass. The newcomers include Dexter Fletcher, Bruna Marquezine, Ed Speleers, Saffron Burrows, Philip Arditti and Bugzy Malone.

Announcing the new season, Ritchie said the ambition of the series had grown, with its fictional world expanding and the consequences of its characters' actions becoming more significant, according to Netflix Tudum.

"The ambition of 'The Gentlemen' has accelerated, the world has expanded, and the consequences carry weight," he said. "A third season felt inevitable, and I'm looking forward to pushing the boundaries of it further."

The announcement follows a turbulent second season in which Eddie moved beyond his initial reluctance to enter the criminal underworld and focused on expanding his empire into Italy while becoming involved in parliamentary politics.

His ambitions, however, strained his business relationships with Bobby, played by Ray Winstone, and Susie, while bringing devastating losses. Although Eddie emerged on top, the season finale raised questions about how far he was prepared to go to protect his position and settle scores.

Lead writer and executive producer Matthew Read said he hoped viewers would question Eddie's capacity for ruthlessness following the events of the previous season.

James similarly suggested that the character's pursuit of revenge could come at the cost of his identity, raising questions about how much of himself Eddie might lose along the way.

Meanwhile, Susie's position has also changed. Scodelario said her character had realised she could no longer depend on her father's name or assume Eddie would remain a reliable business partner, signalling a possible shift in their relationship.

Netflix has not announced a release date for the eight-episode third season.

headline: A date with death, courtesy of 007
description: A date with death, courtesy of 007
author: AFP
article_text:
While the Day of the Dead is a centuries-old tradition in Mexico, its parade over the weekend in the capital is a newer additionwith thanks to Bond, James Bond.

The Day of the Dead, when Mexico honours its deceased by blending pre-Columbian traditions with the Christian All Saints' Day, is historically a family affair. Relatives visit cemeteries and set up altars with food and other items their loved ones enjoyed in life.

Then came 007.

The 2015 Bond film 'Spectre' opens with the British spy walking through a crowd dressed as the dead in downtown Mexico City. On Saturday, giant skeletons, floats and performers in feathered headdresses and masks filled the streets of Mexico City for the 10th anniversary of the Day of the Dead parade.

Musicians and acrobats joined the floats, giving the downtown avenues a carnival atmosphere.

Portuguese tourist Ana Suares, 32, called the parade fascinating. "People happy, the costumes, the flowers. It is quite wild! People coming together to remember those who are no longer here but are in our hearts," she told AFP.

Isabel Halsey, a 37-year-old from the United States, put it this way: "It is colourful, smelly, dramatic, full of people of different nationalities and personalities. I love it!"

Miguel Angel Mancera, who organised the first parade while serving as Mexico City mayor from 2012 to 2018, said the procession quickly exploded in popularity. "Everyone started asking me, 'What about the parade? When's the parade?'" he said. "It was an adventure."

City officials expected more than half a million visitors from Mexico and abroad to watch this year's parade, which fell on the same weekend as the city's Formula One Grand Prix race.

Some of the giant figures used in the Bond film appeared in the first parade in 2016. "It's a very, very big thing now," Mancera said. "It's something I'm really proud of."

An 11-story sculpture of Catrinaan elegantly dressed female skeletonstands in the Zocalo, the capital's main square, as part of this year's festivities.

What was once a "more intimate" celebration has become "a mass event," said Roberto Montalvo, an academic at the Iberoamerican University.

Tourists now pack some cemeteries, competing with families for space. "Do we adapt the visit to the ritual, or does the ritual adapt to the visitor?" Montalvo asked.

headline: Dressing up for a slice of fame
description: Dressing up for a slice of fame
author: Reuters
article_text:
HENGDIAN, CHINA

Visitors to China's sprawling Hengdian World Studios are finding a new way to experience the country's film industry: dressing up as emperors, empresses and palace conspirators to star in their own mini-dramas on professional film sets.

Known as "China's Hollywood", the eastern Chinese studio complex, where many of the country's period dramas are filmed, has opened its elaborate sets to tourists willing to pay for a taste of stardom.

In one palace chamber, four women dressed in silk robes and jade hairpins acted out a court intrigue, complete with a slap across the face. After the director called for another take, the performers gathered around their phones, laughing. They were friends who had travelled more than 1,500 kilometres to make their own production.

The studio has expanded into experiential tourism, allowing visitors to shoot scenes against elaborate backdrops, including replicas of Beijing's Forbidden City and old Shanghai streets used in professional productions.

Since the experience was launched in August, more than 2,000 people have participated, according to Hengdian, with bookings filled on most days, particularly weekends and holidays. "During the National Day holiday, I shoot from morning until dark, and there are still guests we can't fit in," said Wang Weili, a director who once filmed 20 groups in a single day.

The attraction reflects a broader shift in Chinese consumer spending, as a slowing economy and prolonged property slump weigh on purchases ranging from luxury goods to household furnishings. Spending on travel, entertainment and experiences, however, has remained resilient, supporting demand for immersive attractions such as live-action role-playing games, historical re-enactments and interactive film shoots.

For 388 yuan ($55) per person, visitors receive professional hair and makeup, costumes, a 30-minute directed shoot and a 90-second edited video. They can choose from more than 20 scripts, most centred on palace intrigue, romance and betrayal.

"When I was a kid, I loved playing director and getting the other children to act out scenes," said Clare Huang, who played an empress in her group's production. "I've always enjoyed this kind of thing, so today a few of us girls get to see what it feels like," she added.

Another visitor, 28-year-old influencer Xie, travelled to Hengdian after watching videos of the experience on social media. She paid 498 yuan ($70) for a solo performance based on an original script. "We don't have proms in China, so now people go out in costume instead," she said. "Everyone is willing to dress up a bit more boldly and show themselves in the best way they can."

For Hengdian, the venture offers tourists more than a glimpse behind the scenes of China's television industry. It allows them to step into the roles, costumes and elaborate settings usually reserved for professional actors, turning a visit to a film studio into an experience of their own.

article_html:
CHINA/ HENGDIAN:

HENGDIAN, CHINA

Visitors to China's sprawling Hengdian World Studios are finding a new way to experience the country's film industry: dressing up as emperors, empresses and palace conspirators to star in their own mini-dramas on professional film sets.

Known as "China's Hollywood", the eastern Chinese studio complex, where many of the country's period dramas are filmed, has opened its elaborate sets to tourists willing to pay for a taste of stardom.

In one palace chamber, four women dressed in silk robes and jade hairpins acted out a court intrigue, complete with a slap across the face. After the director called for another take, the performers gathered around their phones, laughing. They were friends who had travelled more than 1,500 kilometres to make their own production.

The studio has expanded into experiential tourism, allowing visitors to shoot scenes against elaborate backdrops, including replicas of Beijing's Forbidden City and old Shanghai streets used in professional productions.

Since the experience was launched in August, more than 2,000 people have participated, according to Hengdian, with bookings filled on most days, particularly weekends and holidays. "During the National Day holiday, I shoot from morning until dark, and there are still guests we can't fit in," said Wang Weili, a director who once filmed 20 groups in a single day.

The attraction reflects a broader shift in Chinese consumer spending, as a slowing economy and prolonged property slump weigh on purchases ranging from luxury goods to household furnishings. Spending on travel, entertainment and experiences, however, has remained resilient, supporting demand for immersive attractions such as live-action role-playing games, historical re-enactments and interactive film shoots.

For 388 yuan ($55) per person, visitors receive professional hair and makeup, costumes, a 30-minute directed shoot and a 90-second edited video. They can choose from more than 20 scripts, most centred on palace intrigue, romance and betrayal.

"When I was a kid, I loved playing director and getting the other children to act out scenes," said Clare Huang, who played an empress in her group's production. "I've always enjoyed this kind of thing, so today a few of us girls get to see what it feels like," she added.

Another visitor, 28-year-old influencer Xie, travelled to Hengdian after watching videos of the experience on social media. She paid 498 yuan ($70) for a solo performance based on an original script. "We don't have proms in China, so now people go out in costume instead," she said. "Everyone is willing to dress up a bit more boldly and show themselves in the best way they can."

For Hengdian, the venture offers tourists more than a glimpse behind the scenes of China's television industry. It allows them to step into the roles, costumes and elaborate settings usually reserved for professional actors, turning a visit to a film studio into an experience of their own.

headline: Tax evasion: panel seeks recovery of Rs1.12tr
description: Tax evasion: panel seeks recovery of Rs1.12tr
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
A Senate Sub-Committee on Interior and Anti-Narcotics has expressed serious concern over the alleged misuse of the FATA/PATA tax exemption scheme, delays in recovering billions of rupees in outstanding taxes and the failure of several companies to provide required records.

The panel met under the convenorship of Saifullah Abro at the Parliament House.

Abro directed the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR), Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) and other relevant institutions to submit complete documents, determine potential revenue losses and establish responsibility for any violations of the law.

The meeting reviewed the issuance of consumption certificates for imported goods, alleged tax evasion, non-payment of dues, investigations and the performance of relevant departments.

Senator Umar Farooq and officials from the Interior Ministry, FBR, FIA, police and other departments attended the meeting and briefed the Committee.

During the briefing, officials informed the committee that imported goods worth approximately Rs1,120 billion under the FATA/PATA tax exemption scheme were under scrutiny.

Consumption certificates and related records had been identified for goods worth around Rs389 billion, while further details were required regarding the remaining imports, their utilisation and outstanding tax liabilities.

The body was also informed that 223 consumption certificates had been issued to 108 companies. It questioned why complete information about imports, factory production, utilisation of goods and tax payments was unavailable for all companies.

Senator Abro questioned the performance of the FBR, stating that Pakistan was seeking loans from international financial institutions while billions of rupees in alleged tax dues remained unrecovered. He said negligence and delays in collecting taxes were unacceptable.

He declared that public money would be recovered at all costs, adding that national resources belonged to the people and no compromise would be made in protecting them.

If investigations established tax evasion or financial irregularities, those responsible must be identified, legal action initiated and outstanding amounts deposited into the national exchequer, he said.

The convenor directed officials to prepare a separate case file containing import records, customs documents, consumption certificates, tax payments, bank statements and other relevant information.

He also sought clarification about the legal basis and supporting documents concerning approximately Rs85 billion and the requirements fulfilled before the release of imported goods.

Officials explained that companies were required to deposit an amount or pay order equivalent to the value of imported goods with customs authorities before their release to factories, subject to prescribed conditions.

headline: Pakistan, South Korea sign judicial MoU
description: Pakistan, South Korea sign judicial MoU
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
In a significant step towards strengthening international judicial partnerships, the Supreme Court and the Supreme Court of the Republic of Korea on Monday signed Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on bilateral judicial cooperation

According to a statement issued by the SC, the MoU will open new avenues for institutional collaboration, judicial knowledge exchange and technological innovation.

It said Chief Justice of Pakistan (CJP) Yahya Afridi, who is on an official visit to Korea, was warmly received by Korean Supreme Court Chief Justice JO Hee-de at the Korean Supreme Court in Seoul.

The two chief justices held substantive discussions on strengthening institutional relations, fostering mutual learning and exploring opportunities for closer cooperation between the two judiciaries.

The meeting culminated in the signing of the MoU by the two chief justices, marking an important milestone in judicial relations between Pakistan and the Republic of Korea.

The MoU provides a comprehensive framework for sustained institutional engagement, covering judicial exchanges, professional capacity building, judicial education, collaborative research and the sharing of institutional experiences and best practices.

It places particular emphasis on judicial reform and modernisation, electronic court systems, digital justice, artificial intelligence and its responsible use in judicial administration, smart courts, judicial analytics and cybersecurity.

The framework also envisages reciprocal judicial delegations, professional attachments, study visits, expert exchanges, joint conferences and seminars, as well as periodic high-level judicial dialogue.

It provides an institutional mechanism for coordinating and advancing mutually agreed initiatives, thereby translating the commitment to cooperation into practical and sustained engagement.

On the initiative of the Lahore High Court (LHC) chief justice, the Punjab Judicial Academy organized the interactive session attended by more than 125 judges from various districts of Punjab.

During the session, the FSC CJ shared valuable insights on the subject in the light of the Holy Quran and Sunnah. He explained the relevant provisions of the West Pakistan Family Courts Act of 1964 and discussed key judgments and directions issued by the superior courts.

headline: IHC orders regularisation of FIA-NCCIA staff
description: IHC orders regularisation of FIA-NCCIA staff
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
.

The Islamabad High Court (IHC) Monday directed the authorities to complete the process initiated for regularisation of employees of the FIA and NCCIA, and submit a comprehensive report detailing the interviews conducted by the relevant directors and their results.

Justice Arbab Muhammad Tahir issued a written order while hearing petitions filed by Tauqeer Jadoon and others seeking regularisation of their services.

According to the written order, the FPSC submitted its para-wise comments and report before the court.

During the hearing, the additional attorney general informed the court that FPSC approval was a mandatory legal requirement for regularising the employees.

headline: Govt houses illegally occupied, panel told
description: Govt houses illegally occupied, panel told
author: Naeem Asghar
article_text:
A parliamentary panel on Monday called into question the closure of the Pakistan Public Works Department (PWD), alleging illegal occupation of government houses and the failure to provide official accommodation to eligible employees.

The National Assembly's Standing Committee on Housing and Works meeting was held at Parliament House under the chairmanship of Maulana Abdul Ghafoor Haideri.

Committee member Mir Shabbir Ali Bijarani objected to the absence of the minister, secretary and relevant officials, calling for the meeting to be postponed.

The chairman also questioned who would respond to members' queries when neither the minister nor the secretary was present. Officials informed the committee that the newly appointed secretary had not yet assumed charge, while the minister had gone to meet the prime minister.

Expressing displeasure over the absence of the relevant authorities, the committee chairman said no responsible official was present to answer the committee's questions.

During the meeting, committee member Samina Mohiuddin Jamali alleged that private individuals were living in government houses in Islamabad's Sector I-8 and collecting rent from them. She questioned why vacant government houses were not being allotted to deserving government employees.

The ministry's joint secretary confirmed that some of the houses were vacant.

Committee member Malik Abrar Ahmed also said government employees were being denied official accommodation despite making payments, while their complaints were not being addressed effectively.

Protesting against the absence of senior officials, Agha Rafiullah questioned whether such treatment was being meted out to the committee chairman, who belongs to Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F).

He asked what purpose the meeting served when no responsible official was present to provide answers.

The closure of PWD also came under scrutiny, with Hassan Sabir, Syed Sami-ul-Hasan Gillani and Dr Darshan Lal questioning how many investigations, cases and disciplinary actions had been initiated against those responsible if the department had been abolished on account of corruption.

The members pointed out that more than 5,000 employees and their families had been affected by the decision, but there was no clarity about identifying those responsible for corruption or taking action against them.

Haideri said it was unjust to punish an entire department and its employees for the corruption of a few individuals. He questioned why the department had been abolished without completing alternative arrangements, leaving its employees facing difficulties.

headline: Bilal urges embracing financial innovation
description: Bilal urges embracing financial innovation
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
Pakistan must embrace financial innovation and emerging technologies to become a prominent player in the evolving global financial landscape, rather than remain a consumer of technologies developed elsewhere, Minister of State and Pakistan Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (PVARA) Chairman Bilal bin Saqib said on Monday.

Addressing a dialogue on "Digital Assets and the Future of Banking" at the Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS), he said Pakistan needed to play an active role in shaping the rules of the emerging international financial system.

He stressed that digital assets and blockchain technology offered opportunities to transform the country's financial infrastructure, expand financial inclusion and open up investment opportunities beyond cryptocurrency trading.

The discussion was held with Pakistan Banks Association (PBA) Chairman Zafar Masud.

Bilal said Bitcoin had served as a gateway to the wider digital assets ecosystem, while the level of adoption demonstrated the world-class talent of Pakistanis and their ability to adapt to the future of finance.

He said the potential of blockchain technology extended far beyond Bitcoin and cryptocurrency trading, encompassing changes in the movement and storage of value, tokenisation, broader access to investment opportunities and programmable money.

He added that these developments could significantly benefit Pakistan by promoting financial inclusion, making investment opportunities accessible to a wider population and transforming the country's financial infrastructure.

He stressed that Pakistan should become a co-author of emerging global financial rules instead of remaining a consumer of technologies developed elsewhere. He said the country had previously remained outside discussions when international correspondent banking and card payment systems were established, adding that Pakistan continued to bear the cost of that exclusion.

"The question is whether we want to rent our future or own our future," he remarked.

Bilal said Pakistan needed to work closely with banks and the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) to establish an enabling regulatory environment that encouraged innovation without compromising financial stability. He warned that the cost of inaction could be far greater than the risks associated with taking timely and responsible action.

He said they were a lifeline for Pakistan, but much of the international money transfer infrastructure continued to rely on systems established decades ago. Even a reduction of two to three per cent in transaction costs on Pakistan's annual remittances of approximately $41 billion could channel an additional $1 billion into the grassroots economy, he said.

Bilal said Pakistan needed to work closely with banks and the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) to establish an enabling regulatory environment that encouraged innovation without compromising financial stability. He warned that the cost of inaction could be far greater than the risks associated with taking timely and responsible action.

He said they were a lifeline for Pakistan, but much of the international money transfer infrastructure continued to rely on systems established decades ago. Even a reduction of two to three per cent in transaction costs on Pakistan's annual remittances of approximately $41 billion could channel an additional $1 billion into the grassroots economy, he said.
